The obligation itself is still carried in the composed set, because an advisory instruction is recorded rather than hidden. **Three test fixtures had to change to accommodate this, which is itself the finding**: `presence_test`, the `AXC-008` conformance case and one golden row were each constructing an advisory approval while asserting on the composed requirement, so the defect had coverage and the coverage was asserting the defect. `expiry_seconds` is additionally bounded to 60..604800 seconds and **refused rather than clamped** at either end — the upper bound is ADR-065's coordinated approval-and-reservation window, previously enforced only in a package with no production importer, which is a ceiling no deployment actually had.

- **The approval family's "shortest expiry wins" rule had nowhere to put a per-policy expiry** *(Community)* (#3891). ADR-065 states the rule and the retired planner implemented it, but the shipped algebra stamped every composed requirement with the evaluator's single expiry, so a policy demanding a ten-minute hold and one demanding a day were indistinguishable. `expiry_seconds` is now an optional `approval_challenge` parameter taking part in the same minimum as the evaluator's stamp. It is **refused, not defaulted**, on any other family and when carried without an evaluation clock: a value that parsed as zero would win every minimum and expire the challenge at the instant it was issued, and timeout is always deny.

- **The shipped corpus is now ENFORCEABLE: the first anchored production engine, and the per-plane restriction that makes it possible** *(Community)* (#3895). #3967 put the platform's own controls in the model; nothing enforced them. `pdp.AnchorToShippedCorpus()` had **zero non-test callers**, and the only production `pdp.Engine` in a booted binary was the plane-shadow observer's - `Unanchored(...)` by design, compiling a per-observation world with a blanket permission and a synthetic enforcement profile. "The corpus is in the model" and "the model enforces the corpus" were different facts.

  **The measurement that shaped the design.** Wiring the anchored engine and activating the WHOLE corpus on the `decide` plane, then driving a real request: **every request answered ERROR / `unknown_constraint`**. The shipped corpus is the UNION of controls across all planes, and `decide` reads the STATIC substrate only - no dynamic evaluator, no risk scorer, no media pipeline, no region resolver - so four dynamic-substrate constraints resolve UNKNOWN, and supplying every signal as authoritatively absent still leaves `sys_dyn_gdpr` unknown on `principal.region`. **The tempting fix was the wrong one**: a fabricated `false`, or an empty region, makes the ERROR disappear by asserting that a detector positively did not fire when nothing looked - the fail-open the tri-state exists to forbid, applied to the platform's own ceilings. The ERROR was the system telling the truth.

  So an engine on a plane activates the corpus **restricted to the controls that bind there**, DERIVED from two declarations that already record it - the plane's substrates and the detector census's `planes` column - and never from a list anybody maintains. Measured: `decide` 70 of 91, `mcp` 70, `proxy_tier` 70, `orchestrator_response` 69, `cowork_ingest` 69, `wcp` 21. Both arms fire, and the static and dynamic restrictions are proven **disjoint and total** in both directions, so a restriction that silently began dropping a control fails rather than passing quietly.

  **The trust anchor learned what a restriction is.** A second production anchor requires a stated REASON and verifies every system policy in the bundle as **byte-identically present** in the corpus this binary shipped: a control may be left OUT, and can never be added, nor kept by name while its condition, obligations or authority change. An empty restriction is refused outright. All three driven red-first. Against the anchor's stated threat - replacement of the corpus SOURCE - this is no weaker than the whole-corpus check; it does not defend against an in-process caller, which could already hand any document to `NewEngine`, and the code says so rather than implying more.

  **What a fresh install now gets.** A `deployment` authoring vocabulary that is not a fixture: three stage actions welded to the AuthZEN adapter's own table, an argument schema and payload leaves derived from the shipped corpus, trust realms derived from the identity plane, enforcement planes and detectors from their censuses - resolved ONCE as a snapshot carrying its content digest and the registry version a decision and a proof travel with. Plus an explicit baseline permission pack, one permission per registered action, because **an engine activated with the corpus alone permits nothing and would deny every request** - a failure that looks like a working cutover until the first real one.

  **The decision axis gains `enforce` as a storable value and the DEFAULT DELIBERATELY DOES NOT MOVE.** v11's ruling is that the anchored engine is the default enforcer, and this is not the change that makes it so. `enforce` also RECORDS, and every compose file and the marketplace template pass `AXONFLOW_DECISION_SHADOW_MODE` through empty - so flipping the default here would take every upgraded deployment from *no shadow work at all* to *a shadow world compiled and an OPA evaluation run on every governed request at full sampling*, while enforcing nothing, because the per-plane enforcing seam is not wired yet. The value is storable, parseable and recordable now; the default flips with the seam, and the named observable that says so is a **non-test file calling `planeshadow.RegisterEnforcingPlane`** - `TestTheDefaultFlipsWithTheEnforcingSeam` censuses the source for exactly that and fails on the day one appears. It deliberately does NOT read `planeshadow.EnforcingPlanes()`: no boot code runs in a unit test, so that registry is always empty there and a tripwire reading it could never fire. **Amended by PR-A2 (#3895):** the seam now exists on the decide plane, and the default is STILL `off` - by operator ruling rather than by the gap - so that test now pins the one registrar and the `off` default together.

  **BEHAVIOUR CHANGE: `axonflow-policy-import` now requires `-database-url` (or `$DATABASE_URL`) for a DRY RUN as well as for `-write`.** The deployment vocabulary's realm attributes are a fact of that database, so a plan validated against a vocabulary other than the one it would be published into has validated something else. The connection is opened solely to resolve the vocabulary and closed again; the dry run still writes nothing. The refusal names the reason, and the tool's usage block and the operator flow in `technical-docs/designs/TYPED_AUTHORING_PERSISTENCE_AND_LEGACY_IMPORT.md` both show the flag.

  **BEHAVIOUR CHANGE, stated rather than discovered in a release note: a deployment configured with `AXONFLOW_TYPED_AUTHORING_CATALOG=conformance` can no longer ACTIVATE.** The fixture vocabulary may still be validated and published against; enforcing a world no request can arrive in is not a posture, and the refusal names the remedy. `deployment` is the value a real installation sets. Both runtime suites that set `conformance` moved, and their typed documents were regenerated through the real authoring types and proven to validate and publish with their gauntlets before the shell was touched.

  **The vocabulary resolves on FIRST USE rather than at construction**, so it cannot be resolved before this process has finished declaring what it wired - whether a SCIM directory exists decides whether the built-in realms carry a group graph, and getting that wrong gives a deployment a different catalog digest from an identically configured one. Stated precisely because an earlier draft of this entry claimed it fixed a live defect and cited two line numbers as a measurement: traced rather than compared, `initializeComponents()` already declares the directory before the route is built, so resolving at construction would have been correct today. Lazy is kept for the reason that survives the correction - it does not depend on that order staying true. **A failed resolution is deliberately not memoised**, so a transient database error at the first request cannot freeze the wrong vocabulary until a restart.

- **Nine shell assertions could not observe the value they asserted on, because jq's `//` treats `false` as absent** *(Community)* (#3964). The alternative operator yields its right-hand side when the left is `null` **or `false`** — only those two are falsy in jq, `0` and `""` survive — so it is safe everywhere except on a boolean, and on a boolean it destroys exactly the value a `= "false"` assertion exists to see. Found while fixing one instance in `runtime-e2e/1431_policy_path_alias` (#3956); swept afterwards, because a one-instance fix beside a comment stating the general rule is how a class stays open while looking closed.

  **Three shapes, and only the first announces itself.** INVERTED — `ee/examples/scim/user-provisioning` PATCHes `active: false`, reads `.active // true`, and asserts `= "false"`, so a server that deactivates **correctly** answers `{"active": false}`, `//` returns `true`, and the script printed `[FAIL] Failed to deactivate user` on every success; the assertion could never pass. UNOBSERVABLE — `.approved // empty` then `= "false"`, where `approved: false` **is** the blocked case and renders as `""`, so the blocked branch is unreachable and the suite derives its own expectation from a value it cannot read. FAIL-OPEN — `.blocked // false` then `= "false"`, where a response with no `blocked` key at all (an error envelope, a 5xx body) scores as "not blocked" and the assertion **passes**; this is the one that lets a real regression through, and it is silent.

  **The denominator is the point as much as the findings.** 934 jq `//` expressions across tracked `*.sh`, 118 values compared against `"false"`, and **9** of those sourced from a `//` default. Every one of the sites comparing against `"true"` is **safe** — there both a genuine `false` and an absent field fail the comparison, which is the correct direction — so the exposure is entirely on the `= "false"` side. The issue as filed said ten; one, `runtime-e2e/3281_wcp_stepgate_segment`, is a **false positive of the pattern**: its `// empty` operands are array elements inside a larger filter whose result is `length >= 1`, a genuine boolean. Driven, not assumed, and it is an allowlisted row in the new guard rather than a silent skip.

  **A guard, because this is the class's third recurrence.** `tests/regression-test-required/jq_alternative_operator_on_a_boolean_test.sh` fails a shell value read through jq's `//` and then compared against `"false"`, prints the safe `has()` idiom, and carries eight controls: each of the three shapes is caught, the `= "true"` comparison and the `has()` idiom are **not** flagged, a non-jq comparison is not flagged, and a tree too small to be real is an instrument failure (rc 3) rather than a clean result. Run against the tree before these fixes it names exactly the nine, with the one false positive allowed.

  **Not exercised at runtime.** These are shell assertions in live suites and examples; the fixes are proven by driving `jq` against fixtures in both directions, and no suite was executed for this change. Two of the touched suites — `runtime-e2e/2642_gateway_precheck_audit` and `runtime-e2e/2705_sensitive_data_lever` — and `ee/examples/scim/user-provisioning` are referenced by **no workflow at all**, so they run in no job today; that is #3940's class one directory over and is stated here rather than discovered later.
- **Three Go modules in the tree did not build, and no job built any of the 132** *(Community)* (#3940). The reason each survived is the same and it is the durable half of this change: `unit-tests-example-modules` discovers `examples/` and `ee/examples/`, the root-module arms cover their own packages, and **nothing covered `ee/platform/*` nested modules, `runtime-e2e/*`, `platform/cmd/*` or `scripts/key-rotation`**. A module could land there broken and stay broken silently — two of the three were even RECORDED as broken in `go-module-dispositions.tsv`, with no lane that would notice if that ever changed in either direction.

  **The issue's three modules were not the three that were broken, and the count matching is what makes that dangerous.** `runtime-e2e/2563_obligation_pep/pep_harness` was already fixed on `main` by #3878's PR, and `runtime-e2e/p2b_ingest_classify_enrich/cmd` — which reached `ee/platform/scarf-client` transitively with no require and no replace — is a fourth the issue's census could not see. Same number, different membership, and nobody re-derives a set whose count still matches.

  **A new lane, `Build: Every Go Module`, builds all 131 non-excluded modules, and its discovery is an EXCLUSION RULE rather than a list of roots.** `git ls-files '*go.mod'` is the whole tracked tree minus whatever `.gitignore` already removes, so a module added under a directory nobody thought of is discovered the day it lands. `nested_module_discovery_test.sh` moves from the roots `ee/` and `examples/` to the same rule, which is what put `runtime-e2e/` in scope at all; its control fixture had the identical defect — it seeded only those two roots, so every row for a module outside them read as stale inside the fixture.

  **The rule is "builds under at least one tag set", stated in the lane with its reason.** `ee/platform/license-server` depends on `//go:build enterprise` code and correctly cannot build with plain tags; a plain-tags-only sweep flags it, and the answer is not an exemption row but asking the question the tree can answer. Two more mechanics are recorded where they are enforced: `go build -o <dir> ./...` only where a main package exists (it fails "no main packages to build" on a library-only module, which produced five false reds out of eight), and `sed -e 's#/go\.mod$##'` rather than `\?`, which is a GNU extension that leaves BSD sed's output unchanged and reported **all 132** modules broken.

  **`marketplace-subscription-handler` had three layers, not the "missing go.sum entries" the issue reports.** It pinned `service/sesv2 v1.32.7`, a revision that has never existed upstream, so `go.sum` could never be generated at all — the dispositions row already said exactly that, one layer deeper than the issue. Beneath it the source did not compile: it imported `marketplacemetering` while the only reference is a commented-out `ResolveCustomer` block. the dead `marketplacemetering` import is gone and `tidy` dropped its require with it, so the module now carries **no** marketplacemetering dependency - #3980's implementer must add it back pinned to `v1.36.4`. `sesv2` resolves to `v1.73.0`, the only sesv2 pin in the tree. **The metering call is still a TODO and this change does not add one** — #3980.

  **`ee/platform/orchestrator/llm` is deliberately NOT fixed**, and its row now says why rather than repeating a symptom. Adding the require the issue asks for produces an **ambiguous import**, not a build: its `go.mod` declares `axonflow/platform/orchestrator/llm`, which shadows a real package inside the platform module. `ee/go.mod` replaces a path this directory does not declare, so the replace is inert and nothing can reach its 16 files, and `platform/orchestrator/Dockerfile` records "EE orchestrator modules: none, all seven are built from `platform/` (#3252)". It is orphaned, making it build would make dead code look alive, and it wants a delete-or-revive decision.

  **One further defect the widened scope exposed:** `unit-tests-standalone-modules` kept its exemptions in an inline `EXEMPT` variable — a second exclusion set over one tree, which is the exact shape `go-module-dispositions.tsv` exists to end. It now reads that file, byte-identically in `test.yml` and `test-community.yml`, and its single exemption is a row.

- **A licensed Enterprise deployment could read `Community, 2 nodes` from its own database with nothing saying so, and node three onwards was then recorded as a licence violation** (#3957 item 1). The licensed tier reaches the database through exactly one path — `promoteDeploymentOrgTier` at agent boot — and nothing checked that it arrived. Migration 094 seeds the deployment org at `tier='Community', max_nodes=2` with `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`; the licensed values arrive only through that call, whose failure is logged and deliberately non-fatal. **Absence is detectable; a plausible wrong value is not.**

  The consequence is not the portal badge. `platform/agent/node_enforcement/monitor.go:121` reads `organizations.max_nodes` and writes a row into `node_violations` for every node past the cap, so a fully licensed deployment holding `max_nodes=2` records node three onwards as infringing. The portal's licence page, its node pages and its admin tier read the same row.

  **Filed under Community because the code ships to the mirror** (`platform/agent/license_tier_sync.go`, `run.go` and a `core/` migration all reach it) even though the *effect* is on licensed deployments: a community deployment validates no licence, so no promotion is attempted and the new `/health.license_sync` member is omitted entirely rather than reported unverified.

  **A shape the audit does not name, and it is why extra logging would not have been enough.** `promote_deployment_org_license` wrapped its whole body in `IF EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_name = 'organizations')`. When that guard was false the function **returned successfully having written nothing** — `db.Exec` reported no error and the agent logged `✅ Synced licensed tier`. A success line for a write that never happened, and nothing about the Exec result could distinguish it. The guard was also unqualified by schema while the `INSERT` targets `public`; `core/175` qualifies it.

  **`core/175` adds a helper that reports the row it wrote, and the read is INSIDE the function on purpose.** The obvious fix is a `SELECT` in the agent after the call. That rests on a precondition nobody had established: `organizations` carries FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY (mig 103) — which binds the table OWNER too — under a policy keyed on `app.current_org_id`, a GUC the migration connection never sets. If it were false, a caller-side read-back would return zero rows on a **healthy** deployment and the agent would report "the licensed tier reached nothing" every boot; a guard that fires on healthy deployments is one that gets switched off. It could not be settled by reading the tree, and that is worth stating because it looks settled: migrations 146, 148, 149, 151 and 165 all read `organizations` unfiltered after 103, and **every one of them is silently satisfied by seeing nothing** — 146 loops over zero organizations, 149 counts zero orphans, 145 only warns. Vacuous negatives. Moving the read inside the `SECURITY DEFINER` body removes the dependency rather than assuming it: whatever lets the `INSERT` happen lets the `SELECT` see its result, and if the owner cannot see the row the `INSERT` could not have happened either. **Measured on a real Postgres**: with `SECURITY INVOKER` the same call as `axonflow_app_role` fails with `new row violates row-level security policy`, so the posture is load-bearing and not decoration.

  The outcome is published where a machine reads it: `/health.license_sync` beside the in-memory `tier` it can now be compared against, and `axonflow_license_tier_db_sync_verified`. The gauge is keyed on **the verification, not on the call returning** — a gauge set from `err == nil` would be #3957 item 2's defect (`policySetSource` reporting `"database"` on the first successful *load* regardless of whether the *seed* worked) wearing item 1's number. It stays non-fatal: the in-memory tier is already correct, so a transient database hiccup must not stop a licensed deployment serving.

  **`runtime-e2e/2535_org_tier_promotion` is now WIRED, and what being unwired cost is measured rather than argued.** The suite has existed since #2535 carrying `unwired — CI-eligible; needs an executor`. This change renamed the boot log line it waits on, in **three** places; two were updated and the readiness wait in `boot_agent` kept the old spelling, so every licensed boot would have hung for ninety seconds while the assertions it gates all passed. Nothing reported that because nothing ran it. The marker is now declared **once** and read everywhere, matching both spellings so the suite reads a pre- and post-change binary. Its `health_field` helper did a single-level `.get()` and returned the empty string for a dotted path, so an assertion on the nested `license_sync.verified` would have read `""` forever — found by reading the helper rather than trusting it. The suite gained the assertion floor a wired suite requires (6, verified by running it, not assumed), and the unwired ceiling in `lint-runtime-e2e-executors.sh` drops 135 → 134 so a new unwired suite cannot silently take the slot this one vacated.

  Driven both ways on a real Postgres with a real Enterprise licence and the real migration chain: 6/6 with this change, and against an agent built from `main` the row assertions pass while **both** `license_sync` assertions fail — a pre-change agent promotes correctly and has no opinion to report.

  **Three more pre-existing guards caught this branch, and one of them caught a decision being overturned that was already settled.** The suite's workflow first carried a `pull_request` trigger, reasoned from first principles about cost (two Go binaries against a Postgres service, no image build). `no_pr_trigger_for_stack_booting_suites_test.sh` censuses every stack-booting workflow and refuses exactly that, because the 2026-09-03 measurement showed the two opt-in gates cut **zero** — everyone opted in — and it offers an ALLOW list keyed on MEASURED per-run minutes, which a local estimate is not. The worry that sent it there (a `merge_group`-only suite never runs, because merges are admin-merges) was answered by something not found first: `nightly-e2e.yml` is the routine coverage for this tier and selects by a property, with the correctness inputs living in `.github/nightly-suite-paths.yml` — where the suite is now registered, so it runs against main whenever one of them changes. The workflow also gained the `relevant` job that scopes a merge-queue entry, since `merge_group` takes no `paths:`. The migrations gate's wiring ratchet caught the branch too; the three `TestMigration175_*` proofs are registered in it.

  **And the capability census caught the #3840 class again.** `platform/shared/capability`'s `route_exemptions` are keyed on `file:LINE`, so editing `run.go` invalidated seven rows at once — with **two different deltas in one commit** (`/health` moved −1 because a block above it shrank, the `/metrics` family +12 because the health member was added above them). The rows are remapped by matching each one's registration EXPRESSION and its ORDINAL rather than by nearest line, because the two `/api/clients` rows are distinguishable only by order and a proximity remap could silently swap their reasons. The line-keying itself is filed rather than fixed here: re-keying a shared guard mid-flight, while other lanes may be editing the same file, is its own change.

  **R3 round 1 blocked this and found two defects that were mine in the way that matters: both are the failure mode this change argues against, relocated into my own instruments.**

  The Prometheus gauge's Help text said *"Absent when no promotion was attempted"*. **A registered plain Gauge is never absent** — it gathers as `0`, which the same Help text defines as "attempted and does not match". Every Community, community-SaaS and central-agent deployment, and every licensed one during boot, exported `0`, so an alert on `== 0` would fire on **every healthy deployment**. That is precisely the fire-on-healthy criterion the read-back design is argued around, moved one layer up into the metric. It now registers lazily on first publish, so "absent" means what it says.

  And **nothing distinguished "reports the row it wrote" from "echoes its arguments"** — the claim in this change's own title. Replacing the migration's `RETURN QUERY` with `SELECT p_tier, p_max_nodes, p_expires_at` passed every pin, all the sqlmock tests and the live e2e, because in all of them the argument and the stored row hold the same values. The discriminator is a row that *differs*: a `BEFORE` trigger forces the stored tier to Community while the call asks for Enterprise, so a helper that reads reports Community and one that echoes reports Enterprise. Verified red on that mutant, and the test checks the trigger is actually attached before believing anything it implies.

  **Corrected before release (#4007): the reporting helper is a NEW name, and the old one stays exactly as migration 142 defines it.** `core/175` first redefined `promote_deployment_org_license` in place, changing its return type from `VOID` to `TABLE`. Two things broke, and neither could be seen because this lane could not run (#3972). Its unqualified `COMMENT ON FUNCTION` became ambiguous wherever the pre-142 overload was still live, failing the whole migration on the 142→133 upgrade path with `function name … is not unique`. And redefining 142's own signature with a different return type made **migration 142 un-re-runnable** at the fully-migrated state — `cannot change return type of existing function` — which seven migration tests in `platform/agent` rely on, because re-running up and down at the current schema is what makes a `_down` usable for incident rollback. The body now lives under `promote_deployment_org_license_returning`; the old name keeps 142's signature and `RETURNS VOID`, forwarding to it. One promoter body, two names — the original argument against a second helper was against a second *body*, and it still holds.

  **Two of my own instruments were vacuous until a mutation exposed them, and that is the honest record.** The first version of the gauge test asserted absence in the per-test registry — a registry nothing registers into eagerly — so it *passed with the defect planted*; it now asserts absence against `DefaultGatherer`, which is what `/prometheus` exports and what eager registration poisons. And the migration's new PUBLIC-EXECUTE assertion **aborted the apply on a healthy schema**: the fixture omits mig 098, so `axonflow_app_role` does not exist, the role-probed `REVOKE` never runs, and PUBLIC legitimately keeps the post-CREATE default — 117 and 142 guard theirs identically and call it "installed but unbound". Asserting it unconditionally turned a deliberate, precedented shape into a boot-blocking failure. It is now bound to the same condition as the `REVOKE`, checks both halves where the role exists, and was re-proved to fire on a planted `GRANT EXECUTE … TO PUBLIC`. The `search_path` pin and `INTO STRICT` were verified as written by the same apply.

  Also corrected: a claim in this change's own PR body that "nothing on this board should be read as real-PG coverage". `migrations-gate.yml` runs on `pull_request` and executed all the migration proofs on a real Postgres — I asserted that negative about a workflow I had myself edited without reading its triggers. The dark arm is `test.yml`'s alone.

- **A deployment in the non-community posture served STRICTLY LESS than an Evaluation one on the workflow checkpoint surface: a documented resume route was on no router at all and answered the mux's `text/plain` 404** (#3953). **This is filed under Community because the fix is in `platform/orchestrator/workflow_control/handlers.go`, which ships to the community mirror, and because the mirror can reach the defect**: `isCommunityMode()` is false when `DEPLOYMENT_MODE` is UNSET (the #3096 fail-closed default), so a mirror deployment that never set it took the enterprise registration branch and lost the route with everybody else. `POST /api/v1/workflows/{workflow_id}/checkpoints/resume` is registered by `RegisterEvaluationRoutes` and `.../{checkpoint_id}/resume` by `RegisterEnterpriseRoutes`; `run.go` calls exactly one of the two per deployment. `docs/api/orchestrator-api.yaml` described both unconditionally and the first one's summary said "Evaluation and above". **A deployment upgrading Evaluation → Enterprise silently lost a working endpoint.**

  **The fix is structural, not a second registration.** `RegisterEnterpriseRoutes` now CALLS `RegisterEvaluationRoutes` and adds the resume-from-any-checkpoint route on top. These had been two independent copies of the same three approval routes; one copy grew a fourth and the other did not, which is how the defect arrived and how it would arrive again. A superset built by construction cannot drift into a subset. Enterprise gains `POST .../checkpoints/resume` — a capability it should always have had, and one Evaluation already exercised, so the handler and service path are unchanged and already covered.

  **The durable half is that nothing could SEE this, in either direction.** Both directions of the #3949 route-parity guard were green throughout, and correctly so by their own rule: the path IS registered — in a function this deployment never calls. The census reads source and unions the two registrars, so a route present in *either* read as present. `platform/orchestrator/openapi_route_posture_parity_enterprise_test.go` reads the one piece of control flow that decides posture (run.go's `isCommunityMode()` branching), attributes every registration to the registrar that makes it — a new `fn` field on the census's own registration record — and compares the per-posture path sets. **The two directions are deliberately asymmetric:** an Enterprise-only route is ordinary and is held by an allowance row with a stale-row ratchet; a COMMUNITY-only route has no allowance and nowhere to put one, because a higher tier serving less than a lower one is never right. **It is keyed on (METHOD, path), not on path** - "Community can READ it, Enterprise can also WRITE it" is the natural shape of a tier split, and a path-keyed census unions the two verbs and reports the write half as served everywhere. Keying on the method took the real population from 7 restrictions to 12, each with its own allowance row and its own reason.

  Two things the census has to resolve without a type checker, and both are load-bearing: `cost.Handler` and `workflow_control.Handler` **both** declare `RegisterEnterpriseRoutes`, so the receiver variable is resolved through run.go's own `var` block rather than keyed on the bare method name; and postures propagate along the delegation edge, without which this change's own fix would read as the defect it removes — which the control asserts by applying the delegation to a planted fixture and requiring the finding to disappear.

  **The guard found a fail-open in itself on its first run, in exactly the shape it exists to close.** Keyed only on the registrar function, it classified the whole `/api/v1/agents` family as served by both postures — that family is registered DIRECTLY in run.go's body inside `usageDB != nil && !isCommunityMode()`, so its enclosing function is called by every deployment and the function key says "both". Registrations are now additionally classified by line range against the branch they sit in, that answer wins over the function key, and the planted fixture carries the direct shape in both branches. Cutting the line-range arm reds three assertions, two of them on the fixture and one on the real `/api/v1/agents` allowance going stale.

  Both instruments — the source census and a runtime test that builds the Evaluation and Enterprise routers and compares them directly — were driven against the **pre-fix** registrar and each reported `/api/v1/workflows/{}/checkpoints/resume` by name.

  **And so was a third, against a live Enterprise stack.** `runtime-e2e/3281_wcp_stepgate_segment` — which already boots the exact posture the defect lived in and already drives the by-id resume route — gains two assertions: the resume-from-last route is served, and the *same* route on a nonexistent workflow is refused by the HANDLER in JSON rather than by the router in `text/plain`. The second is the discriminator the first cannot be, because it does not depend on checkpoint state - and it keys on the envelope's `code` **and on the message naming the workflow**, not on "the body is JSON", because the obvious version would stop discriminating *silently* the day #3952 lands a JSON `NotFoundHandler` on this router. Nothing above the route can name the workflow. Against the pre-fix registrar both fail with exactly the signature the issue reported: `HTTP 404 content-type='text/plain; charset=utf-8' body: 404 page not found`. The first version of that leg set its shell variables inside a command substitution and died on `unbound variable` under `set -u` — found by running it, which is the whole argument for executing an e2e leg rather than reading it.
- **Five governance policies existed in no migration, and nothing would have reported their absence** (#3786, #3957). `sys_media_nsfw_block`, `sys_media_violence_warn`, `sys_media_biometric_log`, `sys_media_pii_block` and `sys_media_sensitive_doc_warn` were seeded ONLY by `platform/orchestrator/db_dynamic_policies.go`, on the application connection, with the caller treating a failure as `log.Printf("Warning: ...")`. They have no in-memory fallback, so a stack whose seed failed has no NSFW blocking, no violence warning, no biometric logging, no media PII blocking and no sensitive-document warning - and `policySetSource` reports `"database"` on the first successful LOAD regardless of whether the SEED worked, so the metric that exists to catch this reports healthy on a deployment that has none of them. `migrations/core/173` seeds them as the owner, idempotently, on every deployment mode. The Go seeder is deliberately left in place: both are idempotent on the same identifiers, so they cannot disagree, and removing it is a change to a running orchestrator's boot path that belongs with #3565.

- **The customer portal resolved its authoring edition from a variable its container was never given, so an Enterprise deployment silently lost the two-person rule** *(Community)* — introduced by #3943 (`da33c5f5f`) and caught the same day by the post-merge runtime suite: `Portal Parity E2E` was green at 09:45 and red at 18:45. #3943 made separation of duties edition-conditional, which is correct — PRD 5.3 rules it None/None/Full, and the unconditional rule was what made the Community ladder unspendable. `license.ReadCurrentTier` reads `AXONFLOW_LICENSE_KEY` **from the calling process**, and the portal's compose service and its CloudFormation task definition each enumerate their environment without naming it. So on an Enterprise deployment the portal read an empty key, resolved Community, and reported `separation_of_duties: false`. **One author could publish a policy and activate it alone on a deployment whose licence says two people are required.** The smaller, visible half was `GROUP_SCOPE_NOT_IN_EDITION` refusing a group-scoped publication an Enterprise customer had paid for.

  **The fallback is now asymmetric, and the asymmetry is the point rather than uniformity deferred.** Folding an unreadable tier onto Community is right for a **construct** — you lose a capability, you do not lose control, and refusing instead would take a deployment from the smallest boundary to no authoring at all. It is wrong for a **duty rule**, because "fewer capabilities" and "fewer approvers" point in opposite directions: the same fallback that is conservative for the first is permissive for the second. `authoring.ProfileForUnestablishedTier` carries the Community CONSTRUCT set and the Enterprise DUTY rule — the lowest edition for what may be authored, the highest for who must sign it off. Both directions are asserted on one response in one test, because asserting the refusal alone proves nothing (an unresolvable approver refuses too) and asserting the duty alone would pass on a uniform fail-closed that grants constructs it should not.

  **A genuine Community deployment still publishes with one administrator**, which is the whole of #3907 and is the negative twin of the fix. "Unreadable" is not "absent": `platform/shared/authoringedition` separates three signals the licence read alone cannot — a key that VERIFIED (established, at its tier), a key that was present and REJECTED (forged or expired: unestablished), and NO key, split by whether `DEPLOYMENT_MODE` is enterprise-entitled. No key on `community` is a Community deployment saying what it is; no key on `enterprise` is a process that cannot see its licence. The mode NEVER grants: an entitled mode only ever ADDS the second-approver requirement, exactly as `tier_limits.go` rules that mode "may narrow what a build registers, it never grants a limit". The one case this deliberately cannot see — a deployment entitled to Enterprise that declares no mode at all — is stated at the resolver rather than left for a reader to find; every shipped compose file and both CloudFormation templates set one.

  **There were TWO surfaces resolving an edition and each carried its own copy of the read** — the portal and, since #3943, the orchestrator route. Same code, two processes, one of them missing its input, and no amount of correctness in the orchestrator's copy could say anything about the portal's. There is now one resolver. `authoring.NewAPI`, `NewStore` and `PublishOptions` take a `Profile` instead of an `Edition` for the same reason: three separate re-derivations of a profile from an edition existed, and all three dropped the fact that decides the duty rule. The unestablished state is reported on the wire as `constructs.tier_established`, so an author refused a construct can tell "this deployment is Community" from "this process cannot see its licence" — the same refusal, completely different remedies — and every unestablished resolution increments `axonflow_authoring_tier_unestablished_total{cause}` and logs once per cause.

  **A guard, because the runtime half makes the consequence safe and not right.** A portal that never receives the key still loses constructs an Enterprise customer paid for, and nothing at runtime can give that back. `platform/shared/authoringedition` now carries three checks whose populations are DERIVED rather than listed: the binaries that resolve an authoring edition come from the source tree (every file importing the resolver, folded onto its nearest Dockerfile), and every compose service and CloudFormation container definition running one must be given `AXONFLOW_LICENSE_KEY` — modelling compose's overlay merge, since the base file legitimately supplies it for the agent and the orchestrator and supplies nothing for a service it does not declare. A syntactic census keeps `authoring.EditionFor` callable only from the resolver, so a future surface cannot fold a licence read onto an edition itself; it follows import aliases and refuses a dot import rather than reading one spelling. Each half is proved able to fail by planting the shipped defect back and watching exactly its own check red.

- **The orchestrator's typed-authoring route was unreachable on every stack this repository can boot, and on every stack the marketplace template deploys** *(Community)* — `AXONFLOW_TYPED_AUTHORING_CATALOG` reached the `axonflow-customer-portal` service in `docker-compose.enterprise.yml` and no other service in any compose file, and `CustomerPortalTaskDefinition` and no other task definition. #3943 added the community write route to the ORCHESTRATOR and wired the variable nowhere for it, so the surface answered 503 naming the variable on every deployment. This is why `Policy Path Alias E2E` fails on `main` with `typed-authoring publication legs did not run - no vocabulary configured on this stack`: that suite is right, its stack really did not carry what it needs, and it fails rather than skips by deliberate design. The variable now reaches the orchestrator in `docker-compose.yml` and in `OrchestratorTaskDefinition`, and the suite's own harness sets it in the env file it writes — the precondition is part of the suite's setup rather than something a stack is assumed to have. It is **not** covered by the guard above, and the reason is stated there: a process missing it answers 503 naming it, on every endpoint, immediately, so the failure announces itself; a process missing the licence key answered every request successfully under the wrong boundary.

- **The platform's own shipped policies are now IN the policy model, which they were not** (#3884, under #3786, implementing ADR-065's 2026-09-07 amendment). The detector census landed in #3827 and, in that issue's own words, had *"no runtime consumer - it describes the corpus; it does not move it"*. This is the code that moves it, and the honest bound on what it changes is stated first because it is easy to overstate - and the first version of this sentence overstated it in the other direction. **`pdp.NewEngine` IS reached in production**: a booted agent constructs an engine on every shadow world build (`run.go` -> `initDecisionShadow` -> `planeshadow.Bootstrap` -> the observer's `worldFor` -> `shadow.NewWorld`). What makes that path unaffected is that the construction is `Unanchored(...)`, so both new activation guards return nil on their **first line**, unconditionally and independently of any data - exempt by CONSTRUCTION rather than by unreachability. The only production caller of `pdp.Engine.Decide` is that same observer, which RECORDS. So moving the corpus into the model **does not change what any deployment enforces today**. It makes the corpus exist in the model, durably, with provenance and with every divergence enumerated. That is the prerequisite for the cutover, not the cutover.

  **`platform/decision/registry` is the census's runtime consumer.** It embeds `detectors_census.tsv` and registers all 101 rows as `DetectorRecord`s - create-only, for the reason `RegisterAction` is: reclassifying a detector from algorithmic to pattern would disarm a checksum on every document that selects it, with no document edited and nothing to see in any policy. A census row that will not register is a build failure naming the row, which is what makes "a row nothing consumes" impossible rather than merely discouraged.

  **A record declares THREE plane sets, and the difference between them is the whole point.** `Planes` is where a detector is evaluated at all, `GatingPlanes` where its implementation gates every evaluation, `MixedPlanes` where a plane's NAME covers call sites that do not agree - and what is left is where the implementation is in the binary and does not run. All twenty algorithmic detectors carried `proxy_tier` in that last set: the only static call site there was the tier engine's `EvaluatePolicy`, which called `re.MatchString` and consulted no validator, so the Luhn check did not gate `sys_pii_credit_card` and the Aadhaar label requirement did not gate `sys_pii_aadhaar` (#3963 closed it; #4253 then retired the plane). **The direction is OVER-detection and it is worth stating, because the obvious reading is backwards** (#3963): a validator can only REMOVE a match - both of `PatternEvaluator`'s call sites discard the match when it returns false, and there is no path by which one adds a match the pattern did not produce - so an ungated plane reports a SUPERSET, and any sixteen-digit string is a credit card there. The plane over-blocks with false positives; it does not miss detections. The refusal is also expected to become obsolete and says so at the refusal: the tier engine's omission is unwired rather than incapable - the validators are plain exported functions with no receiver and no state, in a package the agent already depends on - the operator has ruled the inconsistency is closed rather than accommodated, and on that day every algorithmic detector gates there and this arm stops firing on its own. `Catalog.CheckDetectorSelection` refuses an inspection policy that selects such a plane, and refuses a mixed plane under a SEPARATE code because the remedy differs: a bare plane needs the policy narrowed, a mixed plane needs the plane split, which is a defect in the legacy plane taxonomy rather than in any policy.

  **One derivation in there is easy to get exactly backwards and is called out in the code.** The census's `validator_planes` column is a property of the PLANE - which evaluators are validator-bearing at all. A record's gating planes are a property of the DETECTOR. They coincide for an algorithmic row and do NOT for a pattern row, because a pattern gates wherever it runs, `proxy_tier` included while that plane existed (#4253 retired it), since the pattern is what both engines ran. Copying the column onto a pattern record would report all 81 pattern detectors as ungated there and make the selection check refuse eighty-one correct policies while the twenty that need refusing looked identical. Both directions are pinned by tests and both were proven red by mutation.

  **The class was re-derived against the running binary rather than taken from the TSV**, three ways, none of them a copy of a resolution rule. The census derives the class through a four-line REPRODUCTION of `PolicyLoader.getValidatorForPolicy`, because the real one is unexported - and those four lines decide whether twenty checksums are armed. `platform/shared/policy/detector_implementation_derivation_test.go` calls **both real functions with real receivers** and holds them equal over all 101 rows; drives every algorithmic row through the evaluator with a probe the pattern matches and the validator rejects; and re-derives each implementation site through `runtime.FuncForPC` on the function value the evaluator returned, comparing it to the census. The instrument carries its own control in the same test over the same probes - a second evaluator with validators disabled must return a match, and the test fatals rather than reporting an ungated row as gated.

  **The shipped corpus is a checked-in typed document with a build-time trust anchor.** `platform/decision/pdp/system_corpus.json` carries the platform's own controls as a system-root document plus an organization-root template, generated by `legacycompile` from a capture of a migrated database and held byte-identical to a fresh build by a real-Postgres test. `pdp.SystemCorpusDigest()` is its digest, exposed exactly as `HelperDigest()` already exposes the tri-state helper module's and for the same stated reason, and **`NewEngine` refuses any system-root bundle whose source digest is not the compiled-in one.** The anchor is a digest and not a public key deliberately: for content that ships inside the binary a vendor signature would be a second and weaker supply chain beside the one already delivering the twenty Go symbols the corpus names, and it would need an answer for an absent signature in CI that is either a tree that does not build or a checked-in key that can sign a platform ceiling. An engine declares its anchor explicitly and an unset one is REFUSED; the three unanchored callers - shadow, replay, conformance - each say in words why. Design and revisit condition: `technical-docs/designs/SYSTEM_ROOT_SIGNING_AUTHORITY.md`.

  **The corpus splits on editability, and that is forced rather than preferred.** the 70 immutable system-tier static rows become the system document, beside 21 policies from the system-tier dynamic rows; the 31 platform-seeded but customer-editable tenant-tier rows become the organization template, of which 22 produce a policy and 9 - the disabled integration seeds - survive as registered detector records instead. The split is because a row a customer may edit cannot live in a build-invariant artifact without removing an edit right they have today, and a per-deployment artifact would give the platform's corpus one digest per deployment. Recorded on #3786 as the answer to its first operator question. **22 rows change authority root as a result** - every enabled tenant-tier static row - and every one is a declared divergence: `staticRootFor` routes a row whose tenant is `global` to the system root, so all 22 sat there. The count is not maintained beside the corpus: `TestTheRootChangeIsAccountedForRowByRow` holds the declared moves EQUAL to the organization template's contents in both directions, so it falls out of the artifact. An earlier build double-counted the dynamic rows and this prose said 32; a count nothing reproduces is worse than a stale one.

  **A corpus policy is plane-independent, and every collapse is enumerated per row.** The shadow compiler emits up to nine policies for one legacy row because its job is to reproduce a per-plane engine; carrying that into the target model would migrate the defect ADR-065 names in its own problem table. The corpus takes the most restrictive plane's compilation and re-keys it, so what a policy SAYS is `legacycompile`'s answer and the only thing decided here is which plane's answer survives. **40 rows resolve more than one action across planes and each carries a `plane_action_collapsed` divergence** naming the actions in play and the winner; 10 rows produce no policy and carry `row_not_represented` rather than vanishing - the nine disabled integration seeds survive as registered records with `enabled=false`, so enabling one is a configuration change rather than the arrival of a control nothing described; 22 carry `root_disagrees_with_tier`. A row-by-row before/after against a real database FAILS on any difference the build did not declare.

  **The plane rule has a caller, and since #3965 it has nothing left to report - which is the outcome, not a gap.** Nothing in the TYPED model selects a plane, so the only surface that can ask *"did this detector's implementation gate on every plane this row ran on"* is the migration, where the legacy planes are still known. `BuildCorpus` asks the registry BY SELECTION, through the same `CheckDetectorSelection` the rule is enforced with rather than a second computation that agrees. When this lane began, **all 20 algorithmic rows carried a `detector_ran_bare_on_some_planes` divergence** naming their own implementation and the planes that ran it bare; #3965 then wired the proxy-tier engine to the validator resolver and that class is now **empty**. The check that reports it was rewritten as a two-directional relationship against the registry rather than a count, precisely so an empty set is a measured agreement and not a builder that went quiet: a divergence the registry derives and the artifact omits fails it, and so does the reverse. Without the call the plane rule would have been a public API with no caller - the same defect as a census with no runtime consumer, one level up.

  **The corpus collapse ranks every declared legacy action and REFUSES what it cannot rank**, which is the one place it deliberately does not mirror the engine. `agent.ActionRestrictiveness` ranks five of the ten declared legacy actions and returns zero for the rest - `deny`, `log_only`, `route`, `alert` and `allow` all sit BELOW `log` - and the shadow model mirrors that on purpose. A migration that inherited it would collapse `deny` and `log` to `log` and ship a weaker control than the row it came from. The five the engine does not rank are placed here and FLAGGED as declared rather than derived, so a collapse decided by one of them says so in its own divergence.

  **Rebased onto #3965 and #3962, and four tests written to go red on exactly that landing did.** None was made to pass. The two-engine `proxy_tier` test was **inverted** to assert the engines now AGREE (#4253 later deleted it with the tier engine) — a disagreement is a fact about a defect, an agreement is a fact about a fix, and it reds if that wiring or the left-context window is ever removed. The bare-plane assertion becomes its mirror image. The plane-refusal arms move to **synthetic** records, because the shipped corpus no longer contains a bare or mixed plane to exercise them and an invariant that cannot fail for the class under test is not evidence about that class; "the shipped corpus has no bare or mixed plane" is now asserted separately, as the different fact it is. The bare-plane artifact check becomes a two-directional relationship against the registry rather than a count, so a builder that went silent fails it from the other side.

  **And #3962 retired one of this change's own artifacts, exactly as it said it would.** `migrations/core/173` now seeds the five `sys_media_*` rows, which is the REVISIT WHEN written into `application_seeded_controls.json`: *"on that day a migrated capture contains these rows and this file is the thing to delete."* It is deleted. What replaces it is the equality that still matters — the migration and the still-live Go boot seeder write those rows **twice**, idempotently, and nothing held them equal; `TestTheMediaSeedMigrationAndTheBootSeederWriteTheSameRows` parses the migration's SQL and compares it to the seeder's literals field by field in both directions, on every tier including the one with no database. The boot-delta arithmetic is retired with it: migrated and booted now hold the same set, so the delta it pinned no longer exists.

  **Five governance controls existed in no migration when this lane started, and a corpus built from a migrated database shipped without them while reconciling perfectly.** The `sys_media_*` policies were written only by the orchestrator's boot path, with the same `tier='system', enabled=true` predicate the immutable subset uses, and `migrations/core/153`'s down file excludes them by name as "the Go seeder's" — so the migrations knew they existed and deliberately did not own them. Measured on this lane's own capture: **10** system-tier dynamic rows where a booted deployment held **15**. This change carried them as data so the corpus could contain them; **#3962 then landed `migrations/core/173`, which seeds them, and that inventory is deleted** (see above). What survives is the finding and the guard it produced: the seeder's list is hoisted to a package-level `systemMediaPolicies` so a test can read it — a list a test cannot read is a list that drifts — unexported, because that reason is satisfied inside the package and exporting it would make what the boot path seeds writable from anywhere in the binary. The two writers are now held equal field by field, in both directions, by parsing the migration's own SQL.

  **A false premise in an existing instrument is corrected rather than worked around.** `platform/agent/system_policy_count_realpg_test.go`'s header said *"System-level policies live ONLY in the SQL migrations - there is no Go-side seed any longer"*. It is false, and it is why nobody noticed that the test cannot see part of the population it appears to count. The header now says what is true and its numbers are labelled as the MIGRATED counts. The test that pinned the migrated-versus-booted arithmetic is **retired rather than kept**, and by its own stated condition: `migrations/core/173` seeds the five rows it measured the absence of, so migrated and booted now hold the same set and the delta it pinned no longer exists - an invariant that cannot fail for the class under test is not evidence about that class. What survives is the writers-agree guard above, which needs no database, and the constants themselves, which #3970 moved 80 -> 85 under an operator ruling; this branch asserts against them and deliberately does not move them, so that two PRs never move one published number.

  **The `proxy_tier` behaviour is also DRIVEN, not only derived.** The registry's record of it is three layers of derivation, every one a reading of the source. `platform/agent/proxy_tier_bare_pattern_test.go` (deleted with the tier engine by #4253) put one input through BOTH engines and observed the disagreement: `4111111111111112` matches the credit-card pattern and fails Luhn, the shared engine returns no match, and the tier engine returns `block`. A Luhn-VALID card is the control and must be found by both, so a failure cannot be about the pattern or the row shape. It also states that it is expected to change when #3963 lands, so the next reader revisits rather than rediscovers.

  **R3 round 1 found sixteen things and every one is fixed rather than noted.** The load-bearing ones: an enterprise-tagged caller in ANOTHER module was never updated for the new required `EngineConfig` field and would have gone red after the merge on somebody else (a missing struct field always compiles, so build, vet and lint were all clean) - `TestEveryEngineConfigDeclaresASystemCorpusAnchor` now censuses every `EngineConfig` literal in the tree with `go/parser`, which reads a file regardless of its build constraints, and that is the property the type-checking alternative does not have. An anchored engine with NO system bundle activated and every check passed, which is a deployment enforcing zero platform ceilings; the absence is now its own refusal and the test that asserted the old behaviour was correct is the test that would have kept it. `deriveEditions` tested one enterprise marker of three, in the fail-open direction. The artifact told an auditor that `sensitive_data_control` - an ENABLED row redacting salary, SSN and medical-record fields - "survives as a registered detector record", which is false in both halves, and threw away the compiler's own reason (`legacy_scan_drop`, #3397); divergences now carry the compiler's reasons and say per row what actually survives. `SystemCorpusOrganizationTemplate` handed out a shared writable document whose documented use is to be extended. Two doc comments claimed guarantees that did not exist - a delegation that was a second copy with no callers, and two consumers of `Editions` that are not written yet - and one cited a test that had never been written, one file away from the mechanism this branch built to prevent exactly that. All are pinned by tests; the `SignalPath` duplication is closed by making the migration tool call the registry's encoder rather than spell it again.

  **R3 round 2 found fourteen more, all fixed, and three of them were defects in round 1's own fixes.** A cross-check that compared `SanitizePolicyID` with `registry.EncodePathSegment` became `f(x) == f(x)` the moment round 1 made the first delegate to the second - upper-casing the hex escape inside the encoder left every suite green - so the encoding is pinned by a written-out table now. `TestCorpusRowByRowBeforeAndAfter` asked only whether a divergence was declared, never which KIND: relabelling all forty `plane_action_collapsed` as `action_unrankable` in the builder passed, while the test's own comment claimed it required a divergence "NAMING it". And the `EngineConfig` census was evaded by `import xpdp "…/pdp"` - a name-based match is under-inclusive on an alias in exactly the way it is over-inclusive on a bare identifier, and only the second was stated; it resolves each file's own import bindings now.

  **The most consequential one is a nullable column.** `migrations/core/030` declares `tier VARCHAR(20) DEFAULT 'tenant' CHECK (tier IN (...))` with **no `NOT NULL`**, and a Postgres CHECK passes on NULL. The corpus asked "did a captured row match this key" and treated that as "did that row carry a tier", so a NULL tier fell through to the organization root and emitted **no divergence of any kind** - a platform-owned control becoming customer-editable on a fully green board, and unreachable by the static-only census if the row is dynamic. An empty tier is now its own declared divergence.

  Also: the organization template's copy was one level deep, so obligations, break-glass lists and condition trees were still shared - eight of its policies carry obligations, and a copy that protects the one field a test pokes is not a copy. `CheckDetectorSelection` returned `UNKNOWN_DETECTOR` for a registered record that inspects no content. `DetectorRecord.Validate`'s header deferred plane validation to the catalog and the catalog did not do it. The `row_not_represented` branch keyed on `policy_id` without the table, twenty lines below a guard that explains why that is unsafe. The divergence sort was not stable. `"signal.detector."` was spelled three times. Five prose claims were wrong, including one naming a symbol round 1 had just unexported and one asserting "one policy per legacy row" where the artifact carries 91 from 85 - both now pinned by tests rather than by prose.

  **Nineteen controls were mutation-proved, each mutation verified present AND COMPILING before its red was believed** - fifteen before R3 and four more on the guards R3's findings produced, including a re-run of the exact mutant that survived round 1 (a validator that accepts every probe, resolved for a pattern row), which the strengthened check now kills. Two needed a second attempt and both are worth recording. One survived because the defect was in the TEST rather than the code: it appended to a returned slice, and `append` on a slice whose length equals its capacity allocates, so it passed against a deliberately un-cloned accessor - an index assignment writes through the shared backing array, which is the aliasing that actually reaches the catalog. The other was a mutation that was present and compiled and did not reach its target: making `ValidatorForPolicyID` return nil does not disarm `sys_pii_credit_card`, because the `pii-global` category default IS `ValidateCreditCard`. Mutating the gate itself killed both tests.

- **Community and Evaluation can author a policy at all, which they could not before, and the reason was not the one the issue title says** (#3907, implementing the #3906 ruling). The edition ladder gives Community 20 customer-authored typed policies and Evaluation 50. There were three separate reasons none of them could be spent, and only the first is the obvious one.

  **There was no route.** `platform/decision/authoring` was imported by exactly one transport, `ee/platform/customer-portal`, which is Enterprise and always will be — #3907 does not propose a Community portal and this does not add one. There is now a typed-authoring write route in the ORCHESTRATOR: `/api/v1/typed-policies/{edition,validate,publish,activate,active}`. The orchestrator because it already owns customer policy writes, already carries the tier-admission wiring and already has the org-scoped session; the agent is the enforcement plane and authoring behind it would put authorship on the request path. A CLI is not an alternative and is sequenced after rather than dropped: `platform/cmd/axonctl` is a separate Go module with its own `go.mod` and no dependency on the platform module, so a CLI is an HTTP client of this route.

  **Separation of duties was applied on every edition, and this is what actually made the ladder unspendable.** `checkSeparationOfDuties` refused any publication whose approvers did not include somebody other than the author; `checkActivationActor` refused activation by the author, and `checkActivationAuthority` additionally required the activator to be a recorded approver. None was conditional on anything. The PRD rules compound approvals and separation of duties **None / None / Full** (section 5.3), so a single-administrator Community deployment could not have published one policy given a route and a durable store as well — the refusal is upstream of both. Below the Enterprise floor a publication may now name no approver and the author may activate their own version. **Nothing else is relaxed**: the document is still validated, still runs the full five-gate gauntlet, is still signed, is still admitted only after verification, still advances a version, still follows the parent chain, and every activation still records a named, non-zero, correctly-typed principal. An unattributed activation is refused on Community exactly as on Enterprise, with its own test, because that is the audit trail and not the duty separation.

  **The limit read zero, keyed on a column the new model does not have.** `OrgPolicies` moves 0/0/unlimited → **20/50/unlimited**, and — the substantive half — the ceiling is now reached from the path a customer actually writes through, keyed on the POLICY rather than only on the legacy `tier == organization` column.

  **The UNIT is a policy, not a document, and that is stated because it is invisible otherwise.** PRD section 6's row absorbed the old "active tenant policies" row, whose unit was a legacy table row — one policy — so a policy is what it counts. The first version of this keyed admission on the DOCUMENT id, which was wrong in the direction that is hard to see: `Store.Promote` refuses "to promote document %q over active document %q under one authority root; a root carries ONE document", so an organization has exactly one active document and a per-document ceiling never binds. W1-C measured the same thing from the import side — **25 legacy rows folding into ONE document carrying 25 rules, nothing refused** — and the drive here had been measuring it green for a second reason worth recording: twenty publications of documents that all carried the same two rule ids wrote **two** ledger rows, because admission is idempotent on the key. Counted in envelopes, 20 would have been in the limits table, in the feature matrix, in the capability census and on the edition endpoint, and enforced nowhere. #3893 had already said so — *"count ACTIVE rule entries transactionally, not document envelopes or lifetime identifiers"* — and the envelope half of that sentence is the half this originally missed.

  The consequence is deliberate and is the reason the unit is worth naming: a deployment holding more than 20 legacy rules **will** exceed Community's ceiling on import. That is a statement about whether 20 is the right number, which is Product's, not a reason to pick a unit that makes the ladder vacuous. It cost nothing while the legacy model was the only write path and would have cost everything the day the typed model became the only one. The admission dimension keeps its name and its wire code: `org_root_policy` is in `migrations/core/171`'s CHECK constraint, in every row already written, in the metric label domain and in `ERR_TIER_LIMIT_ORG_ROOT_POLICY`, and renaming it would be a migration and a contract break to correct a name that is not inaccurate — every policy it counts genuinely is organization-root. The legacy tenant-tier budget (`TenantPolicies`) is deliberately left beside it: v11 is the release where both models run so customers can migrate, and collapsing the enforcement now would need existing rows backfilled into an append-only ledger, which v12's removal of the legacy path makes unnecessary.

  **The edition boundary is CONSTRUCTS, not the signing root** — #3906's correction, and the premise this is built on. `authoring.Profile` bounds four things and **every row cites a PRD row**, so a reviewer checks the table against the ruling rather than against anyone's judgement: group scope (5.2, nested group graph, None/None/Full), separation of duties (5.3), obligation families (5.1 route restriction None/Full/Full; 5.3 approval and budget None/None/Full), and the request-context predicate allowlist, expressed over `contract.Namespace` — a closed set that exists so "the trust class of a term is lexically visible in the policy text" — giving Community `principal`/`action`/`resource`/`args`, Evaluation `env`/`signal`, Enterprise `agent`/`state`. Both classifications are held TOTAL over the contract's own vocabularies by test, so a family or namespace added there and not classified here fails a named assertion instead of defaulting to permitted. A construct with **no ruling** is RESERVED to Enterprise under its own code, `CONSTRUCT_HAS_NO_EDITION_RULING`, kept distinct from "your edition does not carry this" because the two have different audiences: one is an upgrade, the other is a question for whoever owns the PRD. One construct is in that state today — step-up authentication, which no PRD row names.

  `PublishOptions.Edition` is REQUIRED with no default, and `authoring.API.Publish` OVERWRITES a caller-supplied edition with the surface's own, so a transport cannot widen its boundary by naming one. The graceful-downgrade exclusion in `admission.recordUnlimited` carried a REVISIT note saying it was free only while the ceiling was zero; the ceiling moved, so the exclusion moved with it in the same change rather than after it — an Enterprise deployment now records customer-authored policies off the request path, so a later licence lapse finds a ledger that describes the deployment instead of an empty one that hands it a fresh full ceiling on top of everything it already holds.

  `authoringcatalog` moves the catalog resolution to one community-visible package with three callers that must agree; two resolutions of "which vocabulary does this deployment author against" is a vocabulary fork whose symptom is a policy one surface accepts and another calls `ACTION_NOT_REGISTERED`.

  **The route was UNREACHABLE in the first draft, and the runtime-e2e gate is what asked for the proof that found it.** The handler is served by the orchestrator and takes its organisation from `X-Org-ID`, which the **agent** stamps from the validated licence — two binaries, two registrations, and only one of them was there. A caller reaching the gateway got 404; a caller reaching the orchestrator directly was refused for want of an organisation. Every unit test and every real-database test passed. `platform/agent/proxy.go` now registers the prefix, and `runtime-e2e/1431_policy_path_alias` — the only executed suite that boots a community-mode stack with the agent in front of the orchestrator — carries the arm that fails in that state.

  **The author fallback is restricted to editions WITHOUT separation of duties**, closing a hazard that is currently unreachable. Where the two-person rule applies, an author who is a client credential and an approver who is a directory user are different *principals* — the comparison is over subject, realm and type and it answers correctly — but they may be the same *person*, holding the credential and their own login, and the rule is about people. It is the same axis error #3876 fixed one step along: that compared a rendered TYPE where it meant subject; this would compare SUBJECT where the rule means human. It cannot arise today only because this route names no approvers at all, so an Enterprise publication is refused before the author is compared with anybody — safety resting on a distant design choice, which the first person to add an approver field here would remove without touching the author resolution. Raised by the v11 master on review; the fallback now exists exactly where its justification does.

  A second reachability defect fell out of the same look. `X-User-ID` is client-assertable and the agent's #2896 identity trust gate **strips** it unless the deployment has declared its identity source trusted, so a route requiring it would refuse every publication on a default deployment — most Community ones. The author now falls back to `X-Client-ID`, which the proxy sets from the validated credential and no caller can forge. The two are told apart by realm and type — a `User` in the trusted-header realm, a `Client` in the api-credential realm — so a reader of the signed provenance can see which asserted the subject. ADR-065 supports the shape: `SubjectClient` is "ATTRIBUTION, not authority … may appear in an actor chain and may be audited", and an author records who wrote a document rather than the authority it is scoped to.

  **Not in this change, and named rather than absorbed.** There is still no durable store — `authoring.Store` is in-process on EVERY edition and there is no document table for Enterprise either, so "Community has no store" was never the distinguishing fact; durability is #3776/#3880's and the core migration for it is allocated. This route names no approver and offers no field for one, so an ENTERPRISE deployment cannot publish through it: that is deliberate and has its own test, because an Enterprise deployment has the portal, which resolves approvers against the organization's own directory, and a second approver-resolution path here would be a second opinion on who may approve a policy.
- **A requester could stay eligible to approve their own escalation, because an approver pool compared a RENDERED principal** (#3878, epic #3555). `identity.ActorChain.Contains` used `hop == p`, and `PrincipalID` is a comparable struct of realm, TYPE and subject - so `EligibleApprovers` did not strike `User::workspace:raj` out of a pool when the request's actor chain named `Agent::workspace:raj`. The type classifies a subject; it is not part of who they are, and the two sides get theirs from different places: the chain's from the request's token, the pool's from configuration `ValidateApproverPool` itself describes as "assembled from several directories". Two sources for one subject is where two classifications diverge. `Contains` is now `ContainsSubject` and compares `PrincipalID.SameSubject` - the realm is still part of the identity and the subject id is still case-sensitive, because a realm's own identifier is opaque and nothing establishes case-insensitivity for it.

  **The correction SHRINKS an approver pool, which is the opposite direction from the rest of its class** (#3876 made a control stricter and the failure mode was somebody told no). Here a deployment whose quorum equals its answerable pool size can go from reachable to `QUORUM_UNREACHABLE`, and an unreachable quorum is an escalation nobody can answer. That consequence is asserted rather than noted: `TestWideningSelfExclusionCanMakeAQuorumUnreachable` pins a pool that stops satisfying a quorum of two and the same pool still satisfying a quorum of one, so a widening that emptied every pool cannot pass as a fix. **No deployment's quorum changes today**, and that is measured rather than assumed - a structural caller census across every module in the tree and both build tag sets finds no reference to `ApproverQuorumReachable`, `EligibleApprovers` or `ValidateApproverPool` outside the identity package, and `AdmitChain` reached only from `VerifyChain`, which nothing calls either. `TestNoProductionCallerReachesTheApprovalAndChainAdmissionPath` is that census, and it FAILS the day a plane wires the surface, with the sizing work that then becomes owed written into its failure message.

- **And one person could BE a two-person quorum, on the same pool** (#3878). Found by the hostile review of the exclusion fix above, and it is the harder half of the same class: nothing deduplicated the eligible set, so a pool naming one subject under two classifications - the exact divergence self-exclusion had to be corrected for, arriving from the same several directories - offered TWO eligible approvers, and `ApproverQuorumReachable` compares `len(eligible)` against the clause's quorum. Fixing the eligibility hole and not this would have closed "the requester approves themselves" while leaving "one person is the whole quorum" open on the same configuration. `EligibleApprovers` now returns one entry per subject, deterministically the first in the sorted order `InteractiveMembers` already establishes, and discloses the collapse in the admission detail for the same reason it discloses an exclusion: a pool that comes back smaller than the configuration says is a question an operator will ask. Two subjects with the same directory id in DIFFERENT realms are not collapsed. `ValidateApproverPool` deliberately does not refuse such a pool at save time - a pool assembled from several directories naming one person twice is untidy configuration, not an unanswerable pool.

- **The same rule keyed on a rendered identifier in two more places, and the third instance was on the live decision path** (#3878). `contract.Request.Validate` detected an actor-chain cycle with `seen[a.ID.String()]`, so `[User::realm:alice, Agent::realm:alice]` was one subject delegating to itself and was admitted as two principals; `identity.AdmitChain` had the identical hole one module over on the same rule, keyed on the comparable struct. Both now key on the identity. The consistency check three lines above the first one - "the chain root IS the principal" - is deliberately left EXACT and says so in the code: it asks whether one producer built one request consistently, and widening it would let a request declare a principal its own chain root classifies differently.

  The rule now exists ONCE, as `contract.ID.IdentityKey` and `contract.SameEntity`, and `authoring.samePerson` delegates to it instead of restating it. It has one branch, in both directions: for `KindPrincipal` the type is dropped and the local part folded, and for every other kind BOTH are kept, because a `JiraIssue::conn:ABC-1` and a `JiraProject::conn:ABC-1` are two resources and the registry keys its catalog on exactly that distinction. A zero identifier matches nothing, including another zero.

- **The class is now enumerated structurally, and a new unclassified comparison fails the build** (#3878). Five instances across three subsystems is a class with a sixth on the way, and the reason is structural: `PrincipalID`'s `==` silently includes the type, so the wrong semantics is what an author gets for free and every one of the five read as correct code at review. `platform/shared/identity/principal_comparison_census_test.go` type-checks every package of every module whose `go.mod` can reach the two identifier types, under both build tag sets, and records every `==`, map key, rendered-form key, equality-helper call, decision-condition literal and identity-helper call over them - 65 sites, each classified `identity`, `classified` or `open` WITH A REASON. It is a typed AST walk rather than a grep because the three known instances were spelled three different ways and a sweep for any one finds neither of the others; the `contract.Request.Validate` instance above was found by it rather than by reading. The scanner is proved able to report by planting five bad comparisons and one clean file into an in-memory copy of the identity package - nothing is written to the tree - and the census's own reporting branch is driven with that planted scan.

  An `open` row is an instance this change does NOT fix and must name the issue that owns it: policy scope targets a rendered principal (#3936), and `authoring`'s scope overlap and containment checks mirror the evaluator on purpose. The census also proves itself on a mirror-shaped tree, where the platform module has no enterprise configuration because the sync strips `platform/orchestrator/ee/`; there it reports that the staleness direction did not run and for which module, rather than reporting a clean tree.

- **The portal's approver dedupe keyed on the rendered form too** (#3878). `ee/platform/customer-portal/api/typed_authoring.go` skipped a repeated approver's directory round trip using `seen[ap.String()]`, so one person named under two principal types cost two lookups. It keys on the identity now. **This is a cost bound and nothing more**: both entries still reach `provenance.approvers`, so a signed publication can still record one person as two approvers, which is #3939 and is pinned by an assertion in this change's own test so that fixing it there has to come past that line.
