Door four is privilege reached through role MEMBERSHIP or table OWNERSHIP, where one statement names no application role and the other names no verb and no table - and an owner is not bound by a grant at all. **Door five is an auto-updatable VIEW, and it SHIPPED SEPARATELY as `migrations/core/174` (#3905) rather than here.** A single-table view with no join or aggregate rewrites `UPDATE`/`DELETE` into writes of the underlying table, executed with the view OWNER's privileges - so it is bound by neither this revoke nor, since the table is ENABLE and not FORCE row level security, migration 018's org isolation. That makes it a cross-TENANT path rather than a privilege one, and it predates this work entirely (`core/014` creates the view, `core/098` grants on it, `core/018` gives ENABLE not FORCE), so it was split out and landed first instead of waiting behind this change. It is named here because finding it is what falsified this migration's original claim to be "the only write path": the value of the strong claim was not that it was true, it was that it was checkable.

- **Five governance policies existed in no migration, and migration 172 would have made that visible only on new deployments** (#3786). `sys_media_nsfw_block`, `sys_media_violence_warn`, `sys_media_biometric_log`, `sys_media_pii_block` and `sys_media_sensitive_doc_warn` were seeded ONLY by `platform/orchestrator/db_dynamic_policies.go`, on the application connection, with the caller treating a failure as `log.Printf("Warning: ...")`. Once `dynamic_policies` is SELECT-only to the application roles that INSERT is refused, so a FRESH stack would silently have no NSFW blocking, violence warning, biometric logging, media PII blocking or sensitive-document warning - while every EXISTING stack already holds the rows, which is why the gap is invisible everywhere anyone would inspect. `migrations/core/173` seeds them as the owner, idempotently, and it is a SEPARATE migration from the revoke because 172's down is a real rollback: a data seed inside it would make that down ambiguous, since deleting the five rows would remove policies every existing stack legitimately holds and not deleting them would mean the down no longer reverses the up. The Go seeder is deliberately left in place - both are idempotent on the same identifiers - and its removal belongs with #3565.


- **Community's typed-authoring route published successfully and lost everything on restart, while the legacy model it replaces persisted** *(Community)* — #3975. `publish` → 200, `activate` → 200, `GET /api/v1/typed-policies/active` → **404 `nothing_active`** after a restart, on a stack whose `static_policies` and `dynamic_policies` rows survived. `deploymode` declares Community as `enterpriseSchema: false`, so `migrations/enterprise/155` never ran there, the three typed-authoring tables did not exist, and the route built the in-process store. **Durability is not the paid feature; organization-root authoring is** — #3906 already withdrew the reading under which "organization root" meant "Enterprise only", and the edition boundary is carried per document by `authoring.Profile` at publication, on the constructs an author may spend, not on which rows a deployment may keep. v11 decision D4 is untouched.

  **`migrations/core/176` creates the same three tables on every deployment mode**, with the constraints, RLS policies, append-only triggers and role-guarded grants `enterprise/155` carried. It is a **measured** no-op on any database that already applied 155, not an assumed one: 155 applied three times to one database gave 0 schema objects before, 15 after the first, and exit 0 with zero ERROR lines and an identical catalog snapshot on the second — with the snapshot **proved able to report a difference** by dropping one policy between reads, and a third application repairing it. Both application orders were driven: core-then-155 and 155-then-core converge.

  **155's DOWN becomes a no-op, which is the load-bearing half.** Two migrations creating one set of tables must not both drop them: on a database carrying both records, whichever rolled back first would destroy the other's state while its own row still claimed to be applied, and the runner skips an applied version before it reads the file. `core/176`'s down is the single rollback path on every edition. It is deliberately **not** conditional on 176's absence — a rollback whose behaviour depends on another migration's presence is two rollback paths under one filename, and which one ran would not be recoverable afterwards. 155's UP is unchanged in what it applies; only its header is corrected.

  **The grant block is in the core file because the census requires it there, not as house style.** `TestEveryForceRLSTableHasAnApplicationGrant` keys a table on the first file in sorted order that FORCES row-level security on it, `core/176` sorts before `enterprise/155`, and its edition arm requires a core-forced table to be granted by a core file — `migrations/core` ships to the community mirror and `migrations/enterprise` does not. Proved by removing the eight GRANT lines and watching the census name all three tables as *forced by core/176, granted only by enterprise/155*, the `customers` shape from #3636.

  **`authoringstore` moves to `platform/policy/` and drops its `//go:build enterprise` tag.** Nothing in it branches on an edition, a tier or a licence — it implements `authoring.Backend` and every rule governing a publication has already run before any method is called — so Enterprise-only was placement, not behaviour. It is **not** co-located with the seam in `platform/decision/authoring` because that would be a module cycle (`platform/decision` is its own module reached by `replace`, and this package imports `platform/agent/rls`); the reason is in the package header so the placement is not tidied into the cycle later.

  **The orchestrator route takes the application-role connection**, and `GET /edition` reports the posture in #3962's vocabulary — `persistence` (`process` | `database`) and `signing_key_custody` (`process`), derived from the workspace the organization actually has through the same call a publish makes. `signing_key_custody` stays `process` even when persistence is `database`, because the private half is per-process and conflating them would overstate what durability buys. **The published contract was updated to match**: the spec declared five properties on that response and the handler returned seven, and the route-parity guards key on (method, path) and never look at response properties, so nothing in CI would have caught it.

  **Durability is claimed only after the whole chain succeeds.** `authoringstore.New` only validates its arguments and never touches the database, so marking a workspace durable from it alone would produce artifacts whose signing key was recorded nowhere — rows that survive the process and cannot be loaded by it, which reads as data loss rather than a stated limit. So it is `New` → `AuthorizeKey` → `LoadTrust` → rebuild over the loaded trust, and only then durable, falling back with a log rather than claiming durability it lacks.

  **And the first version of that made durable storage work exactly once per organization, ever.** The signing key identifier was derived from the ORGANIZATION while the material is minted fresh per process, so the second process presented a new key under an existing id, `AuthorizeKey` refused it — correctly; that read-back is what stops one process taking over another's identity — and the workspace fell back. **#3975's own symptom, reintroduced by its fix**, caught by the restart leg and by nothing else. The same defect had been written a week earlier in the customer portal (#3962). So the derivation now lives in `authoringstore` as `KeyIDFor`, and **`AuthorizeKey` refuses an identifier that does not carry the fingerprint of the material presented with it**: the constructor alone is a convenience a third caller can skip, the refusal is what makes a fourth instance impossible. All three callers were censused before the refusal shipped — the legacy importer already complied and is left alone, since repointing it would change identifiers already stored on deployments. `ErrKeyAlreadyAuthorized` is now unreachable through `AuthorizeKey` but is **kept and proven** for rows written directly, because a check nothing can reach is indistinguishable from one that works.

  **A transient database error used to downgrade an organization permanently, and that is fixed here too.** `workspaceFor` fell back to the in-process store on ANY failure of the durable chain and then CACHED that workspace, so one unreachable moment - a restart, a failover, a connection blip - left the organization in-process for the life of the process, and the next publish returned 200 into memory and was lost on the following restart. #3975's own symptom, reachable through nothing worse than a hiccup, and invisible to every test because they drive a healthy backend or no backend at all. **Once a database is configured, persistence is not optional**: the degraded workspace is no longer cached, so the next request retries; writes are refused with 503 `storage_unavailable` rather than accepted into a store that cannot keep them; and reads are still served. `/edition` reports a THIRD value, `unavailable`, distinct from `process` - a deployment promised durability and not getting it must not read like one that never had a database - and the published contract carries all three. Driven with a durable open that fails once and then succeeds: the first publish is 503, the degraded workspace is not cached, the second publish is 200, and a signing-key row backs the recovery.

  **The authorize-load-rebuild chain now exists once instead of three times.** `authoringstore.OpenForSigning` replaces the copies in the community route, the customer portal and the legacy importer, returning the store, the loaded trust and the key identifier. Copying that sequence without its key naming is exactly what produced the defect above, so the sequence stops being something three callers must remember. The importer keeps its own `import-` prefix and now derives the suffix through the same function the refusal checks against, removing a compatibility that held only while both sides agreed on the slice width and on lowercase hex.

  Two findings from the review are filed rather than fixed here: durable artifacts are not re-gated on edition, so a lapsed licence keeps serving constructs it may no longer author (#3993, consumer S10 #3895); and `GET /edition` has a write side effect, minting and recording a signing key per organization per process (#3994, shared with the portal).

  **Guards, each driven red before its green was believed.** A `go/parser` census requires every `TypedAuthoringRouteHandler` literal to name the new `db` field — a missing struct field always compiles, so the first signal would otherwise be a handler that silently keeps the in-process store — and a second test fails the day any field is exported, because the single-package scan is complete only while no other package can populate the literal. The community restart leg in `runtime-e2e/1431_policy_path_alias` publishes, activates, **proves the orchestrator really restarted via `StartedAt` before/after rather than trusting `compose restart`'s exit code**, and re-reads through the gateway; the surviving activation is matched against the published digest by reading `typed_policy_activations` under the organization's RLS scope, so "loaded back, not re-created" is a row in postgres rather than a field on a rendered document.

- **The gateway pre-check and `/api/request`'s Phase 1 enforce the anchored engine, per organization at `enforce`** *(Community)* (#3564, #4092). Two more scopes have an enforcing seam, after `decide` (#4025) and the MCP response pass (#4065): `POST /api/policy/pre-check` (plane `gateway_request`) and `clientRequestHandler`'s Phase 1 (plane `proxy_request`). **The process default stays `off`**, and an organization that has not opted in receives the response it received before, byte for byte - held by a test comparing every member against the same handler with no observer, no enforcer and no registration.
  - **One request path, not a third seam.** `decide`'s pass is now scope-keyed (`enforceRequestPass`, `decideRequestPass`), so each plane's gate reads ITS OWN registration and a plane supplies only how its decision reaches its wire. The projection is shared and **derives what it may instruct from what the seam declares it delivers**, so the instruction a caller receives and the delivery activation reads cannot come apart: the pre-check tells a request-phase redaction as `requires_redaction`, the instruction the legacy engine has always given, and `/api/request` tells its caller no obligation at all, so an obligation the decision attaches REFUSES the request rather than letting it proceed with nobody told to discharge it.
  - **`/api/request` was decided by TWO engines until #4253, and the record said which one decided.** Phase 2 was the tier-aware engine (`proxy_tier`), which had no enforcing seam and ran whenever Phase 1 did not refuse, so under `enforce` it could refuse or hold a request the anchored engine approved - including on a shipped control the organization's document permits. That verdict was recorded `engine=legacy` under reason `proxy_tier_policy` on the response, the audit row and the enforce-decision counter, never as the anchored engine's.
  - **Both responses carry `engine` and `mode` only under `enforce`**, and every audit row the seam decides carries them in EVERY mode (a pre-check refused BEFORE the seam - kill switch, a validator's block, a segment-resolution failure - carries the resolved mode and no engine, because no engine decided it), because the body omits them for an organization that did not opt in and the row is then the only record of that organization's posture. A pass that cannot produce an anchored verdict answers 503 naming its cause and never falls back to the legacy engine.
  - **What differs from the legacy engine, stated:** detection overrides (#4045) do not reach the anchored engine on either plane, which includes the organization `pii=redact` override behind the India and Indonesia redaction flags on the pre-check; an anchored approval requirement is a refusal on both, so no queue entry is raised and no single-use grant is spent on a request the legacy engine did not decide; and a detector the plane did not run reads UNKNOWN (#4032's class). Phase 1 drops the `admin-access` category for an administrator, and no control either restriction keeps is hidden by that skip - but **for a different reason than a first reading suggests, and the first version of this entry gave the wrong one**. The four shipped admin-access controls spell their category `security-admin` (core/031), while the skip and the plane's admission both name the shared constant's spelling `admin-access`, so the category filter drops those rows before the administrator skip is ever reached. The guard now sweeps on the census's own spelling, asserts the population is non-empty before concluding anything from it, and is proven to red against a planted control - the previous one matched nothing and passed vacuously.
  - **`openai_compatible` was not cut over when #4092 was filed**, because it resolved its user from an empty token on every deployment, so under the retired `enforce` mode every request would have been refused `subject_type_rejected`. It IS cut over in v11.0.0: its enforcing seam is registered at `platform/agent/decision_enforcing_seam.go:143` and the anchored engine authors the verdict of `POST /v1/chat/completions`.

- **`docs/security/decision-shadow-mode.md` no longer says enforcement cannot happen** *(Community)* (#3564). Five statements were true when written and false since #4025 shipped the first enforcing seam: the title's "recorded only", the intro's "it never changes an outcome, and it cannot", "`enforce` is refused BY NAME" (`identity.ParseCompatMode` accepts it; the agent refuses to BOOT with it only where no per-user identity can be verified), "`enforce` cannot be stored" (enterprise migration 156 widened the column's `CHECK` and the admin API's vocabulary matched it), and "turning the shadow off never changes an enforcement outcome" (the process mode is the resolved mode for an organization with no record of its own). Corrected in place; the rest of that document is #3818's queue.
- **`GET /api/v1/typed-policies/active/summary`** answers `{scope, shipped, organization, pack, packs_counted, disabled, total}` for the caller's organization. The count is taken from the same activation the agent enforces on decide: the published document when one is active, and the implicit baseline when none is. Nothing is read from a legacy row.
- **ADR-044 session overrides are retired: the workflow step gate no longer reads a session override, and the session override writes answer `409 LEGACY_POLICY_WRITE_FROZEN`** (#4252, row H7 of #4254, PRD v11 §1.5). The last reader that changed a decision, the agent's tier pass on `/api/request`, goes with #4281 (#4253). The workflow step gate no longer reads `policy_overrides`: the deny-to-allow flip that let an active session override (or a disabled dynamic row with no action) past a deny is deleted, with the `override_applied`, `override_id` and `override_reason` members of the step gate's policy result. `POST /api/v1/overrides` and `DELETE /api/v1/overrides/{id}` write nothing: the proxy-auth (403), per-user identity (401) and tenant (400) guards answer first (the #4279 principle: the guards first, the body never read), and then every caller is answered `409 LEGACY_POLICY_WRITE_FROZEN` naming the organization's typed document; the body is not read. The MCP `create_override` and `delete_override` tools answer the same code and remedy, rendered by the agent rather than proxied (a session on the client-shared identity is still refused for its identity first). Explain's `override_available` is always `false` and `override_existing_id` empty, and the MCP check-input block no longer offers an override. The override reads (`GET`) are unchanged, and a row written before the upgrade stays as the record of what was granted. Plugins whose override tools expect `201` read the `409` from v11.0.0 (their v11.1.0 issues carry the client change). Exceptions, which do not reach the community mirror: the restated `runtime-e2e` suites (3077, 3062, 3426, 3012's comment, and a note on the manual 2759), the customer portal's proxy allowlist descriptions (`ee/`), and the decision records (`technical-docs/`: ADR-044, ADR-060, the ADR index, the detector registry design).
- **`AXONFLOW_HITL_GRANT_TTL_SECONDS` is retired** (#4254, PRD v11 §1.13, §5.1). It bounded the lifetime of a single-use HITL approval grant, which v11 no longer mints (#4253). A set value, a well-formed one included, now refuses the boot of both the agent and the orchestrator, naming the variable and the reason; an empty or blank value boots. The upgrade preflight's check 25 lists it. No shipped compose file or CloudFormation template sets it, so only a deployment that set it by hand is affected: remove it from the environment before upgrading.
- **A HITL approval recorded against a service identity** logs that its review record names the service, not a person. It no longer says the approval will not admit a retry, since no approval does.
- **The orchestrator response plane decides every LLM response on the anchored engine**: one evaluation, for the client credential the agent forwarded, with three outcomes (released as sent, released masked, withheld). The detector layer produces facts for that decision and authors no verdict of its own.
- **A response the plane cannot decide is withheld rather than released**, naming its cause, and a withheld response carries no content: the refusal body and the audit row both carry a substitute.
- **`POST /api/v1/process` answers `engine`, `subject_type`, `policy_bundle` and `verdict` on both its 200 and its 403**; `POST /api/request` repeats that decision as a nested `response_plane` member and answers `blocked: true` when the plane withheld the response.
- **The canonical plane=llm audit rows carry the same decision**, on the allowed, redacted and blocked paths alike.
- **The orchestrator's regex PII detector is removed**. Detection patterns, their semantic validators and context-aware confidence scoring are unchanged and continue to live in the shared policy engine.
- **The tenant-policy list and export return the calling client's own dynamic policies as well as its organization's** (#3894, PRD v11 §1.11). `GET /api/v1/dynamic-policies` and `GET /api/v1/tenant-policies`, and their `/export`, read an organization's rows only where the tenant was the organization's id, so a row whose tenant is the calling client's id was missing from the list and the export while still readable by id: every row a Community client writes, since Community's tenant is the client id and its organization the deployment's, and in Enterprise the rows an API client writes whose client id is not its organization's id. `PolicyRepository.List`, which the export pages through, now reads `tenant_id IN (the caller's tenant, its organization)` on the organization pass, and never `'global'`, which the global pass reads once; row-level security still selects the organization. No caller loses a row it listed before. The behaviour was the same at v10.2.0, so this is not an upgrade regression. Rows another client id of the same organization wrote are still listed only by that client; the organization-wide read is on v11.1.0 (#4249).
- **The legacy tenant-policy export returns only the rows categorised `dynamic-` or `media-`** (#4293, PRD v11 §1.11). `GET /api/v1/tenant-policies/export`, and its `/api/v1/dynamic-policies/export` spelling, filter their result to those two category prefixes and say nothing about the rows they withhold, while the list over the same rows does not filter that way; a row can carry neither prefix, because the policy-CRUD import writer stores one without a category. The policy-CRUD family's export applies no category filter over the same table, but no single legacy read returns everything: each is scoped to the calling client and its organization (the organization-wide read is deferred to v11.1.0, PRD v11 §6), and the platform's shipped system-tier rows come back alongside the organization's. The routes are deprecated and their removal is tracked in #4289; the deployment runbook's v11 upgrade section says so and points at #4293 and the API page.
- **`axonflow_create_tenant_policy` answers the v11.0.0 legacy write freeze by name**. On a deployment whose services connect as the application role, which Community SaaS does, it returns a refusal that names the freeze and the typed authoring route `/api/v1/typed-policies`, instead of a generic "could not create tenant policy" error.
- **The tool's tools/list description says so**, so an assistant is told before it calls. Its input schema is unchanged.
- **Breaking: the orchestrator refuses to boot without a database** *(Community)* (PRD v11 §1.1, #4291). The anchored engine authors every enforcing plane's verdict and reads each organization's typed policy from the database, so an orchestrator that has no database, or whose enforcer cannot be built, stops at boot instead of starting degraded: a process serving an enforcing scope with no enforcer would fail every request closed, an outage that reads as a policy decision. In v10.x the same process started without one, logging that usage metering was disabled and serving the built-in default fallback policy set. The agent already refused on the same ground.
**The workflow step gate, the multi-agent plane, `/api/v1/process` and plan execute decide on the anchored engine.**
- The workflow step gate is decided by the anchored engine. A step type is presented as the shipped action its type maps to (`llm_call` as `llm.completion`; `tool_call` and `connector_call` as `tool.call`; `human_task` as `agent.invoke`). A step type the gate's map does not name is refused as `request_unbuildable`, naming the type.
- The step gate decides for the organization and client the agent authenticated (`X-Org-ID` and `X-Client-ID`, installed on the request at the orchestrator's HTTP boundary). A call that reaches the orchestrator without them is withheld as `subject_unverifiable`. A checkpoint resume is decided for the credential that resumes it, and the checkpoint's client stays the recorded actor.
- The step gate presents no content to the engine in v11.0.0. Content conditions are inert there, as they have always been, because the gate never presented a query. Presenting a step's input is a v11.1.0 row.
- A tenant-authored dynamic policy row, including a segment-scoped one, no longer decides the step gate: v10-authored rules stop deciding until they are imported into the typed document. A segment-resolution outage still withholds the step with policy id `segment_resolution_failed`.
- A v10 segment-scoped dynamic policy row has no v11.0.0 equivalent on the workflow step gate. Do not author a group-scoped typed constraint for the step gate in v11.0.0: the gate does not state the caller's groups, so such a constraint cannot be evaluated there and withholds every step as `unknown_constraint`. Binding group scope on the step gate is a v11.1.0 row.
- On the step-gate response and in the persisted `policies_evaluated` record, each policy entry carries its id, name, action and reason; `risk_level`, `allow_override`, `matched_rule` and `policy_description` are no longer present, because the engine names policies by id and reason.
- The step gate's answer carries `engine`, `subject_type` and `policy_bundle`. Each step-gate audit row, and each blocked row of `/api/v1/process` and plan execute, records the plane, the engine's decision id, and `engine`, `subject_type`, `policy_bundle` and `decision_id` in `policy_details` (PRD v11 §5.7).
- A workflow control service built with no policy evaluator withholds every step, naming the cause as "no policy evaluator is wired to this service, so the step is withheld (enforcer_not_wired)". It used to allow every step. A serving orchestrator always wires the evaluator, so this changes only an embedding or a test that built the service without one.
- A challenge that carries no approval requirement is withheld as `evaluation_failed` (policy id `decision_enforcement_unavailable`) on the step gate, the multi-agent plane and both request routes.
- A step refused for having no subject is counted on `axonflow_decision_enforce_decisions_total` with verdict `unavailable` and reason `subject_unverifiable`, as every other enforcer outage is.
- `POST /api/v1/process` and `POST /api/v1/plan/execute` are decided by the anchored engine, under the workflow control plane. `/api/v1/process` presents `llm.completion` and plan execute presents `agent.invoke`, each with the request's query, for the client credential the agent authenticated. An `/api/request` forwarded to `/api/v1/process` is no longer refused by the legacy dynamic pass.
- Neither route can hold a request for approval. A policy that requires approval refuses the request with 403, and `policy_info` names the reason as "blocked: approval_required: ...", naming the plane that cannot hold; nothing is queued.
- A refused request's `policy_info` names the deciding policy, or the cause when no decision could be reached, in `applied_policies`, and each reason in `required_actions` as "blocked: <reason>". A matched shipped control is named in `applied_policies` by its corpus id.
- `/api/v1/process`'s 403 error text is now "Request blocked by policy" (it was "Request blocked by dynamic policy"). Its 403 carries `engine`, `subject_type`, `policy_bundle` and `verdict`. Plan execute's 403 keeps its text, "Policy blocked MAP execution", and carries the same four members.
- `/api/v1/process` no longer reports a dynamic policy's warn in `applied_policies_detail`, and a dynamic policy's `modify_risk` no longer changes `risk_score`. `risk_score` decides nothing on these routes.
- While the orchestrator cannot read its database, `/api/v1/process` is withheld with a 403 naming `active_document_unreadable`; it no longer decides from the last policy set it loaded.
- LLM routing hints from dynamic route policies still steer the provider of an admitted `/api/v1/process` request. When more than one applying route policy names a preferred provider, the last in priority-descending order wins, as before; which one should win is a v11.1.0 decision.
- `GET /api/v1/policies/dynamic` now lists policies in a fixed order (priority descending, then newest first); it was unordered before.
- The orchestrator states `env.environment` from its own `ENVIRONMENT` only, never from a request's context, so a caller can no longer exempt itself from the shipped debug constraint by sending `context.environment=development`.

### Enterprise
- **An organization with fewer than two eligible approvers may approve its own typed-policy versions, by its owner's recorded choice** (PRD v11 §1.12, #4023). Separation of duties stays the default. The organization owner enables self-approval through `PUT /api/v1/typed-policies/self-approval`, gated on `sso:configure` like the detection-posture settings. `migrations/enterprise/158` stores the setting under row-level security, and each change writes its `admin_audit_log` row (`TYPED_SELF_APPROVAL_SET`) in the setting's own transaction. Enabling is refused once two members could approve, counted by the same check that admits an approver. Whether a self-approval is granted is never stored: the portal answers it at each self-approved publication and at each activation by the author of a self-approved version, from the setting and the eligible approvers at that moment, so a second eligible approver ends the exception without anything being revoked. A self-approved publication names only its author and states a reason, which is signed into provenance and recorded on the typed audit row. The editor asks for the reason when you are the only approver, lets the author of a self-approved version promote it while the exception holds, and shows the owner the setting with its toggle. The orchestrator's authoring route installs no answer, so self-approval does not exist there. The runtime leg is `runtime-e2e/3364_portal_parity/test.sh`.
- **A portal whose typed-authoring store cannot be opened refuses, and no longer caches an in-memory stand-in** *(Enterprise)* (#4271). **Behaviour change.** When the configured durable store could not be opened, for any reason (for example a partial outage, the migration 155 tables missing, or a stored signing key that does not load), the customer portal built the organization's typed-authoring workspace over the in-process store and cached it for the life of the process. A publish then answered 200 into memory and was lost on the next restart, and `GET /api/v1/typed-policies/active` answered `{"active": false}` even after the database came back. Such a workspace is now degraded and is never cached, so the next request retries the open, as the orchestrator's has since #3975 (`ee/platform/customer-portal/api/typed_authoring.go:772`, and not cached at `:837`). While the store cannot be opened, publish, promote, rollback and withdraw answer 503 `storage_unavailable` instead of accepting the write into memory; `/active`, `/artifacts`, an artifact's source and `/diff` answer 503 `storage_unavailable` instead of answering from an empty store; and `GET /api/v1/typed-policies/settings` reports `persistence: "unavailable"`, which the policy editor's preview banner states as a database it cannot reach, where it said documents are held in the portal process. The portal recovers without a restart once the store opens. The runtime leg is `runtime-e2e/3364_portal_parity/test.sh`'s Phase S2: with `typed_policy_signing_keys` unreadable, it restarts the portal and asserts the refusals and the settings answer, then restores the table and asserts, with no restart, the same `/active` answer and artifact list as before the fault.
- **The portal's typed-authoring reads answer a store they cannot use 503, never its error** *(Enterprise)* (#4271). The customer portal answered a store error on `GET /api/v1/typed-policies/active` and on the three reads behind `GET /api/v1/typed-policies/artifacts` (the activation history, the active version, the artifact list) with a 500 carrying the raw error as `detail` and no reason; on `GET /api/v1/typed-policies/artifacts/{digest}/source` with 404 `not_admitted`, so a database failure read as "that digest was never admitted"; and on `POST /api/v1/typed-policies/diff` with 422 `diff_failed`, so an outage read as "your document cannot be diffed". Each now answers the orchestrator's #4255 mapping through one writer, `writeTypedStoreRefusal` (`ee/platform/customer-portal/api/typed_authoring.go:1689`): 503 `key_not_loaded` for an artifact signed by a key this portal has not loaded, 500 `active_unverifiable` or `artifact_unverifiable` for one that does not verify, and otherwise 503 `storage_unavailable`, each with a fixed sentence and the error in the log. A digest the store does not hold still answers 404 `not_admitted`, and a candidate's own diff error still answers 422 `diff_failed`. The portal's promote and rollback keep their 200 when the read-back fails, with a fixed sentence in place of the raw error. The runtime leg is `runtime-e2e/3364_portal_parity/test.sh`'s Phase S: with a typed table renamed out from under a running portal, `/active`, `/artifacts`, `/diff` and an artifact's source answer 503 `storage_unavailable` with nothing of the database's error, `/active` answers 200 again once the table is back, and the portal's log carries the error. The portal workspace that cached a degraded store (#4271's fifth site) is fixed by the entry above.
- **The policy editor starts every new draft from the organization template, and controls the shipped set** (#3746, PRD v11 §1.5).
  - **Template seeding.** `GET /api/v1/typed-policies/template` serves the shipped organization template as the exact canonical bytes its digest is computed over. A new draft is seeded from it, because a published document replaces the template: a template control the draft left out would stop deciding. The editor refuses to publish a draft that does not carry the template, and a template that arrives after an edit is merged into it without discarding the edit.
  - **The platform-controls panel.** It moves into the editor and lists each of the 85 controls once, with its policies. It records in the draft's `system_controls` whether each control stays as shipped, is left out, or, for a static control, takes another action.
  - **The imported draft.** `GET /api/v1/typed-policies/imported-draft` serves the upgrade's imported draft, verified against its digest. `POST /api/v1/typed-policies/imported-draft/dismiss` (`policy:write`) dismisses it, with a `TYPED_IMPORTED_DRAFT_DISMISSED` audit row in the same transaction. The editor offers the imported draft as the new draft, with a banner listing what was carried and what was not.
  - **The dry runs read the posture.** The portal's promote and rollback dry runs read the organization's recorded posture through `posture.Repository`.
- **The banking vertical's policies ship as three typed policy packs, `sebi`, `rbi` and `mas-feat`, and migration `industry/banking/402` retires the rows they replace** *(Enterprise)* (#4141, PRD v11 §1.9, §1.2).
  - **Why.** Migrations `industry/banking/300`, `302` and `401` seeded 34 `static_policies` rows. Under PRD v11 §1.2 a seeded row authors no verdict on a plane the anchored engine decides, so on an `in-vpc-banking` or `saas` deployment those controls had gone silent at the v11 upgrade. The deployment mode now installs the packs, and 402 runs at the same boot.
  - **What moved where.** 27 rows are pack detectors, compiling to 35 controls. The 18 compliance rows keep their actions. The 9 Indian-identifier rows follow the shipped PII posture under `pii-india`: warn on requests, redact on responses, each as its own control suffixed `:warn` and `:redact` (the pincode row logs). 7 rows are dropped with no pack control, because a shipped control already decides the same identifier: `sebi_pan_detection`, `sebi_aadhaar_detection` and the five `mas_*` Singapore rows (`mas_sg_postal_detection`'s pattern never compiled under RE2).
  - **Behaviour.** On a banking deployment these controls decide again, through the anchored engine, and every decision they take part in on `/api/v1/decide` names each pack by digest (`policy_packs`); the MCP request and response passes name no pack yet (#4196). A `require_approval` control on a plane that cannot hold, `/api/v1/decide` among them, is refused `approval_required` naming the plane (§1.13). The 9 identifier controls warn and redact wherever their pack binds.
  - **The identifier controls match.** `rbi_passport_detection` names the label-gated `passport` validator its row resolved. `sebi_bank_account_detection` names none: its row resolved a US routing checksum from its id, which rejects every Indian account number, so that control is live where the row never matched. The other seven identifier detectors resolved no validator as rows and name none.
  - **One pattern is narrowed from its row.** `sebi_high_value_trade_oversight` binds its lakh and crore units to a number before them. The row's bare alternation matched "cr" and "lac" inside any word ("credit", "place", "across"), which as a pack control would have held most ordinary requests for approval.
  - **What does not carry over.** An operator's change to one of these rows (a disablement, say) does not carry over; to tune a pack control, carry it under its `pack:<pack>:*` id in the organization's typed document (§1.5). The pack controls do not bind on the orchestrator's response plane, where packs are not loaded; the shipped `sys_pii_*` rows redact there.
  - **Readiness reports.** The SEBI readiness export and the US-securities supervisory-control inventory count configured policy rows, so neither lists a pack's controls, and each now says so.
- **The portal withdraws an organization's typed document** (PRD v11 §1.15, #3746). `POST /api/v1/typed-policies/withdraw` takes a `reason` under the same `policy:write` authority as rollback, and the typed-authoring section offers the action beside the published versions while one is in force, refusing an empty reason before the round trip. Migration `enterprise/159` admits the kind in `enterprise/155`'s copy of the ledger. The runtime leg is `runtime-e2e/3564_per_plane_enforcement/test.sh` Phase E1b: a portal withdrawal, the decision afterwards under the organization's pre-publication bundle byte for byte, and the promotion after it chained onto the withdrawal.
- **The Marketplace template drops `MCPDynamicPoliciesEnabled` and `MCPDynamicPoliciesConnectors`** *(Enterprise)* (PRD v11 §1.2). `ee/platform/aws-marketplace/cloudformation-ecs-fargate.yaml` no longer declares the two parameters or passes `MCP_DYNAMIC_POLICIES_ENABLED` and `MCP_DYNAMIC_POLICIES_CONNECTORS` to the agent, because a v11 agent refuses to boot with either set, `false` included. A stack update that passes either parameter must drop it from its overrides. The partner template is re-synced to match. The customer portal no longer lists `CONNECTOR_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` among its tier-cap codes, and the enterprise licence's `custom_policy_connectors` is deprecated as on Community.


- **A detection-posture change commits with its audit row, or not at all** *(Enterprise)* (#4017). `PUT` and `DELETE /api/v1/detection-posture/{category}` write the override and its `DETECTION_POSTURE_SET` or `DETECTION_POSTURE_DELETE` row in one transaction, through `platform/shared/detectionposture`. The success row used to be written after the change had committed, best-effort, so a change could stand with its row lost; a failed audit insert now fails the change, and the endpoint answers 500 instead of 200. A failed change is still recorded best-effort. The portal's `admin_audit_log` rows are written by `platform/shared/adminaudit`, with the same columns and address handling as before.
- **A CloudFormation deployment can install a policy pack** *(Enterprise)* (#4168, PRD v11 §1.9). The marketplace template gains a `PolicyPacks` parameter. It is empty by default, constrained to comma-separated pack names, and listed under Feature Configuration. It is passed to the agent task alone, as `AXONFLOW_POLICY_PACKS`: the agent is the one process that installs packs, and the portal and orchestrator tasks carry no pack. `tests/community-saas/cfn_marketplace_policy_packs_test.py` pins the parameter, its pattern and that wiring, and that the community-saas template, which runs a Community image, carries none. The partner copy in `axonflow-install` is re-synced first.
- **The FinCrime pack ships as a typed document** (#4126, PRD v11 §1.9). `ee/policy-packs/fincrime/pack.json` carries the pack's ten detectors, transcribed from the retired seed SQL pattern for pattern, and `document.json` its compiled controls: the four blocks as constraints and the six step-ups as mandatory approval requirements naming the pack's approver group. `AXONFLOW_POLICY_PACKS=fincrime` installs it; the agent image carries it at `/opt/axonflow/policy-packs/fincrime`. On `/api/v1/decide` its blocks deny `explicit_constraint` and its step-ups are refused `approval_required`, because decide holds nothing (PRD v11 §1.13). **Removed:** `seed.sh` and `fincrime_policy_pack_v1.sql`, so nothing writes a `fincrime-pack-v1` row. A deployment that ran `seed.sh` keeps its ten rows: with the pack installed they are not loaded, and without it they still decide on the passes the legacy engine runs.
- **The US-securities examination package reads the FinCrime pack from the audit trail** *(Enterprise)* (#4126, ADR-064 section 6). With the pack installed as a typed document there are no `fincrime` rows to count, so whether the Fraud and Risk Add-on was in force is measured from this tenancy's decisions in the window whose audit record names `fincrime@<digest>` in `policy_packs`. Financial-crime detections match both the legacy `fincrime` control identifiers and the typed `pack:fincrime:` ones. The section gains a fifth outcome: the pack was not in force while detections exist, as records written before the pack was installed produce, and both are reported. **Breaking for readers of `GET /api/v1/ussecurities/exam-readiness`:** `fraud_risk_addon_policy_rows` is replaced by `fraud_risk_addon_decisions`, the number of those decisions, and the portal's banner says what is measured. The orchestrator cannot see the agent's install set, so a deployment with the pack installed and no decision in the window reads not in force (#4164).
- **Typed policy authoring is on for every organization: the per-organization `typed_authoring_enabled` flag is retired** *(Enterprise)* (#3746, PRD §1.5). The flag (enterprise migration 154) gated the portal's typed-authoring API and its navigation entry per organization, off by default. PRD §1.5 makes the typed path how every organization configures policy, so it gated nothing legitimately.
  - **Migration `migrations/enterprise/157_identity_org_settings_typed_authoring_retired.sql`** drops the column. It logs how many organizations had the flag on (or that the count could not be taken) and is idempotent. Its `_down` restores the column as 154 defined it, `NOT NULL DEFAULT false`.
  - **The portal no longer reads or writes it.** The typed-authoring routes answer every organization, and `GET /api/v1/typed-policies/settings` reports the catalog and persistence to every organization. The navigation's Policy Authoring entry and the `/policy-authoring` page are unconditional.
  - **A PUT to `/api/v1/admin/organizations/{org}/identity-settings` naming `typed_authoring_enabled` now answers 400** as an unknown field, rather than being accepted and ignored.
  - **`platform/shared/capability/registry.json`** describes the portal's typed-authoring section as on for every organization, and `.github/nightly-suite-paths.yml` lists migration 157 beside migration 154 among the nightly trigger paths.
- **The legacy Policies page is removed from the customer portal** *(Enterprise)* (#3746, PRD §1.11). Policy is configured through Policy Authoring.
  - **Removed:** `app/policies/page.tsx`, its seven modals and `components/policies/types.ts`, the Policies navigation entry, and the 27 `lib/api.ts` client functions and constants (with the 22 types) that only the page used. The dashboard's policy button opens `/policy-authoring`, and the typed-authoring banner no longer calls the legacy list the enforced surface.
  - **Suites:** `runtime-e2e/3364_portal_parity` retires its Policies-page parity arm (floor 50 -> 33, 55 -> 38 when it boots its own stack) and asserts the removal on the rendered portal: `/policies` answers 404 and nothing links to it. `runtime-e2e/3441_policy_category_vocabulary` keeps its registry legs and retires its page legs (25 -> 9). The Playwright golden flows go from 6 to 5, and `scripts/seed-portal-playwright.sh` drops the row only the deleted flow read.
  - The portal's legacy policy routes, the unified-policies aggregator and the proxy allowlist rows are the next change.
- **The customer portal no longer serves or proxies the legacy policy API** *(Enterprise)* (#3746, PRD §1.11). SDKs keep reaching the deprecated export surface on the agent and orchestrator directly.
  - **Removed from `ee/platform/customer-portal`:** the portal's 78 route registrations under `/api/v1/{static,system,dynamic,tenant}-policies`, `/policies`, `/templates`, `/policy-overrides`, `/unified-policies` and `/policy-categories`, with their prefix guards and their handlers (`api/policies.go`, `api/static_policies.go`, `api/policy_overrides.go`, `api/unified_policies.go`, `api/unified_policies_write.go`, `api/policy_categories.go`).
  - **The 28 orchestrator-proxy allowlist rows for those families are removed in the same change,** so a request for a removed family answers `403 ROUTE_NOT_PROXIED` rather than reaching the catch-all without a permission check. A test pins every removed write path.
  - **The dashboard's Total Policies tile is removed:** it counted the legacy tables. #4152 tracks its return as a count of the organization's active bundle.
  - **`platform/shared/policypath/registration_census_test.go` declares the portal's retired families** and fails if the portal registers one again. `runtime-e2e/3130_portal_proxy_allowlist` asserts the refusal for each family (floor 26 -> 35), and `runtime-e2e/3441_policy_category_vocabulary` retires with `/policy-categories`.

- **The FinCrime policy pack's seeded rows decide on none of the anchored engine's enforcing scopes** *(Enterprise)* (PRD v11 §1.2, §1.9; #4126). The ten rows the retired `ee/policy-packs/fincrime/seed.sh` installed are seeded `static_policies` rows, none of what the anchored engine decides from, so on `/api/v1/decide` they neither decide nor interrupt the detector pass. The pack itself installs as a typed document (#4170), whose controls the anchored engine decides. On MCP `check-input`, `check_policy` and the request pass of `query`/`execute` they no longer decide either: the anchored engine decides that pass. `/api/v1/decide` no longer consults the FinCrime Engine B scorer, and its audit row no longer carries the pack's policy ids or names, `risk_score` or `ml_inference_layer_status`: none of them decided the request. The legacy in-process FinCrime engine that decided the MCP request pass until this change is deleted, with its typed context validation (`fincrime_mandatory_fields`) and its Engine B scorer client: nothing reaches them once the anchored engine decides that pass (PRD v11 §5.8), and no MCP audit row carries `risk_score` or `ml_inference_layer_status` any more. `ee/docs/fincrime/CONTEXT_SCHEMA.md` now names the pack as the one consumer of the context objects, and says that nothing validates them. The Engine B service, `ee/platform/risk-scorer`, has no caller either: it no longer seeds the CI caches, and its deletion is #4218.
- **Correction: the FinCrime pack is delivered as a typed document, and its seed script is gone** *(Enterprise)* (#4126, #4170). #4170 delivered the pack: the pack installs as a typed document through `AXONFLOW_POLICY_PACKS`, `seed.sh` and its SQL are deleted, and on `/api/v1/decide` the anchored engine decides the pack's controls. A deployment that ran the retired script keeps its ten rows: with the pack installed the detector layer does not load them, and without it they decided on the MCP request pass until H1a (#4216) cut that pass over to the anchored engine.
- **Breaking: the FinCrime Engine B scorer's variables refuse boot** *(Enterprise)* (PRD v11 §1.2, §5.1). Engine B ML scoring is retired with the legacy FinCrime engine that called it: nothing in the platform asks the scorer for a risk score. `AXONFLOW_FINCRIME_SCORER_URL` and `AXONFLOW_FINCRIME_SCORER_TIMEOUT_MS` join the retired variables (`platform/shared/retiredenv`), so any non-empty value refuses boot, naming the variable and the retirement.
  - **Migration:** remove both from the agent's environment. The v10.x `docker-compose.enterprise.yml` sets the timeout to `100` by default, so a stack started from that file refuses to boot; this release's file sets neither. The upgrade preflight's check 25 fails a deployment whose agent or orchestrator still sets either.

- **The FinCrime Engine B scoring service is removed** *(Enterprise)* (#4218). `ee/platform/risk-scorer` (the `axonflow-risk-scorer` image, its own compose file and its `risk-scorer-tests.yml` workflow) had no caller once the legacy FinCrime engine and its scorer client were deleted (#4216), and its variables already refuse boot. A deployment that ran the optional scorer image can stop it: nothing reads it.
- **The UPI validator no longer accepts an unknown handle outside a payment context** (#4225). `validateUPIID` ended in a default `return true, 0.7`, so an `@` inside a secret (`SuperSecretP@ssw0rd123`) or a `user@host` token was recorded as a UPI id. Under a recorded `pii=redact`, the gateway pre-check then attached a mandatory `field_redact` obligation for it, and a caller that had not declared `field_redact@1` was denied `unsupported_obligation`. An unknown handle is now a UPI id only beside a payment word, a known bank handle still accepts at 0.95, and the pattern carries the whole domain so an email is refused as one. Two limits are stated rather than hidden: the payment word is still a substring match, so `payload`, `resend` or `occupied` beside an unknown handle reads as payment context (pre-existing, routed to #4122); and a VPA glued to the next word by a dot or a hyphen (`rahul@okicici.Thanks`) is now a known false negative, pinned by the tests. The orchestrator's copy of the detector (`platform/orchestrator/rbi`, wired into the RBI module) had the same defect and carries the same fix and the same tests: the seven payloads #4225 measured, plus the shapes the rule is defined by. The denial of an email under a recorded `pii=redact` comes from the email control's own override, is ADR-065 invariant 8 as designed, and is unchanged. `runtime-e2e/2705_sensitive_data_lever` asserts both measured tables on the production-posture stack: every probe approved under the default posture, and under a recorded `pii=redact` the `@` secret approved with no `india_pii` entry, the corporate emails refused by the email control's own override, and the true VPA still `redaction_required`.
- **The portal logs each refused typed-policy publication or activation, RBAC check and expired session with the organization, and with no person's identifier** *(Enterprise)* (#4023). Every error `api.Publish` returns (validation, the fixture gauntlet, separation of duties), an approver the check refuses, and an activation the store refuses (promote, rollback or withdraw) write `[TypedAuthoring] org="<org>" refused kind=<publish|promote|rollback|withdraw> reason=<code>`. A request refused before those checks, such as a malformed body or a workspace limit, is answered as before, with no line. The RBAC gate's refusal, and its error branch too, now carries the organization in place of the user's email (`[RBAC] permission denied: org="<org>" lacks <permission>`), and the portal's authentication middleware logs an expired session with its organization (`[Auth] session expired: org="<org>"`). None of these lines, the three refusal lines and the RBAC gate's error branch, carries a person's identifier, and the typed-authoring line carries no error text, because the log is shipped; six other portal log lines still carry an email (#4245). The organization is quoted, so a value cannot forge a second line. An absent or unknown session still names no organization, because none can be known. The one path of this change that reaches the community mirror is `.github/nightly-suite-paths.yml`, which selects the new suite's runs.
- **The customer-specific seed bundle is retired** (#4138). A policy bundle under `config/seed-data/` had been applied by hand to one Enterprise customer's database: five `static_policies` rows (read-only write and DDL blocks and a full-table-scan block, checked on the gateway pre-check) and eight `dynamic_policies` rows. The platform now prepares nothing specific to one customer, so the seed file is deleted, and `migrations/enterprise/160` retires what it wrote wherever it was applied: each of the thirteen rows, keyed on its seed policy id, is disabled and its metadata becomes a record of the `enabled` and metadata values it had, a second run changes nothing, and the down restores exactly the rows it marked to exactly those values (`updated_at` records the two writes, and a metadata value that was the JSON literal null returns as SQL NULL). A database the bundle never reached is left exactly as it was. The eight dynamic rows the seed bundle wrote (off-hours, bulk-retrieval and volume anomaly controls) are disabled by enterprise/160, so the loader never reads them; their semantics lived only in the MCP endpoint H1b removed, and #4137 (v11.1.0) is the general capability. H1b is #4242. The thirteen rows' full definitions are recorded on #4137. The container-registry policy prepared for the same customer (`infra/ecr-policies/`) is removed with it; a policy already applied in AWS is live state this change does not touch.
- **The portal's typed-policy dry run takes its inputs from the shared builder** (#4152, #4254). The customer portal's typed-authoring workspace built the same decide-plane inputs as the orchestrator's, line for line. Both now take them from `platform/shared/activationinputs`, so the two cannot drift apart. No behaviour changes.
- **A refusal the caller did not cause no longer trips the circuit breaker** *(Enterprise)* (#4246). The circuit breaker trips a client once it has recorded enough policy violations (#1176: by default twenty in five minutes, `AXONFLOW_CB_POLICY_VIOLATION_THRESHOLD`, settable per tenant through `/api/v1/circuit-breaker/config`), and a tripped client is refused on every plane until the circuit recovers. Two refusals were recorded as violations although neither is the caller's doing: `approval_required` (the engine asked for a person's approval on a plane with no approval hold, PRD v11 §1.13) and `obligation_conflict` (the obligations the matched policies attach conflict, which is how the policies were authored). `/api/request`'s segment fail-closed deny (ADR-060), an availability outcome, recorded `segment_resolution_failed` with no gate at all. The rule every recording site applies, `violationFeedsCircuitBreaker` (`platform/agent/decision_enforcing_seam.go:1588`), now exempts both codes and `evaluation_error` (the request could not be evaluated). #4253 removes `/api/request`'s segment gate, and the segment deny with it, so no segment deny reaches the breaker. At decide, the gateway pre-check, the OpenAI-compatible route and `/api/request` the rule for `evaluation_error` is now explicit and changes no outcome: no engine deny with that reason names a policy, so none was recorded. The deny itself is unchanged: the caller gets the same reason, and the site's decision audit row still records it; only the breaker feed stops. The runtime leg is in `runtime-e2e/3329_fincrime_pack/test.sh` (floor 35 -> 44): at the shipped default and with no configuration changed, twenty `approval_required` denies on `/api/v1/decide` leave the client untripped and a twenty-first request is still decided, and twenty `explicit_constraint` denies trip it. `runtime-e2e/3360_pii_action_posture/test.sh`'s comment put the threshold at five; it is twenty.
- **`/api/request`'s agent pass no longer holds a request for approval** *(Enterprise)* (#4253). Its hold was raised only by its retired second pass: a `require_approval` tier row or legacy override held the caller 403 `require_approval` with an `approval_request_id`, raised a `hitl_approval_queue` entry and spent a single-use grant on the retry. With the pass gone nothing the agent's pass decides sets a hold, so the hold exit is removed; where HITL is enabled, a plan the route forwards to `/api/v1/plan/execute` can still pause on the orchestrator's dynamic `require_approval` policies. That includes the organization template's shipped hold, `eu_ai_act_high_value_transaction` (EU AI Act Article 14: high-value bookings flagged for human oversight), which the tier engine held on `/api/request` and which decides nothing there until holds return. Removed with the exit: the agent's enqueue and grant helpers, `axonflow_hitl_policy_enqueue_total`, `axonflow_hitl_grant_consume_total`, `approval_request_id` on the response (and in `docs/api/agent-api.yaml`'s `ClientResponse`) and the audit row's `approval_enqueue`, `approval_request_id` and `approval_grant_id`. An anchored approval challenge is a refusal on this route, as on decide. `AXONFLOW_HITL_GRANT_TTL_SECONDS` is retired with the grant and refuses boot (#4297); holds return with the orchestrator's typed approval challenge (#4254). The legacy import (`axonflow-policy-import`) plans `proxy_request` by default; `-plane proxy_tier` is refused as an unknown plane.

- **The customer portal refuses the retired decision-mode fields** *(Enterprise)* (#4100, removed). `PUT /api/v1/admin/organizations/{org_id}/identity-settings` answers 400 naming `decision_shadow_mode` or `decision_shadow_planes`; there is no per-organization decision mode to record. The columns (enterprise migrations 150, 153 and 156) stay in the schema, neither read nor written, and are dropped in v12: during a rolling deploy a v10.4 portal, which writes both by name, still runs against the migrated schema.

- **The customer portal refuses the retired `compat_mode`** *(Enterprise)* (PRD v11 §1.3). `PUT /api/v1/admin/organizations/{org_id}/identity-settings` answers 400 naming the retirement when the body carries `compat_mode`; the upsert no longer writes the column, and the read and the response no longer carry it. The column stays, unread, until #4165 drops it.

- **An identity outage is always reported as an outage** *(Enterprise)*. A revocation check or a key set that cannot be consulted, on the per-user token validators and on the customer portal's SSO login, is reported as unavailable (`ErrRevocationUnavailable`, `ErrJWKSUnavailable`) and never as an invalid token, including when a later validator rejects the token by shape (an HS256 token in an organization with OIDC configured, where the resolver used to return the last rejection). The status stays `401`. Before, that wording applied only while the identity-compat mode ran, and never on the portal's SSO login.

- **The `DecisionShadow*` CloudFormation parameters are removed** *(Enterprise)*. `DecisionShadowMode`, `DecisionShadowPlanes`, `DecisionShadowSampleRate`, `DecisionShadowWorkers`, `DecisionShadowQueueDepth` and `DecisionShadowMatchLogEvery` are gone from both templates, with the task-definition variables they fed; the old templates defaulted the mode to `'off'`, a non-empty value the new binaries refuse. CloudFormation rejects a stack update that passes a parameter the template does not declare, so remove them from parameter overrides; `update-stack.yml` already skips them. The decision-shadow canary stack keeps its template and names and is repurposed as the enforcement canary's traffic source; its deploy input still defaults to `off`, and renaming it is #4120.

- **v11 is the decision plane, with no decision mode: the product definition is recorded** *(Enterprise)* (#3746, #3566, #3564, ADR-065). `technical-docs/product/PRD_V11_POLICY_DECISION_PLANE.md` and ADR-065's 2026-09-11 (third) amendment record the operator ruling that v11 ships the ADR-065 decision and identity plane as THE system on all twelve planes - no `off`/`shadow`/`enforce` mode, no per-organization opt-in or opt-out, no old-vs-new comparison, the legacy verdict engines unreachable in v11, their code deleted where easy or important in v11 and the rest in v11.1 - with the shipped set enabled under observing actions by default and per-policy enable/disable/action control for every organization as the core control surface, and credential-only callers admitted as the credential principal. Documentation only: nothing in this entry changes a verdict. It supersedes every earlier CHANGELOG statement that a plane enforces "per organization at `enforce`" or that "the process default stays `off`".

- **The marketplace template declares the licence transition to the two enforcement planes** *(Enterprise)* (#4094, #3592). `AgentTaskDefinition` and `OrchestratorTaskDefinition` gain `AXONFLOW_LICENCE_TRANSITION`, driven by the existing `IsLicenceTransition` condition - the same condition, the same two tasks, so a stack cannot be half transitioned. The customer-portal and performance-testing tasks are excluded, as they are from the `DEPLOYMENT_MODE` override, and that exclusion is asserted rather than implied.

- **Security: the customer portal no longer loses audit rows from IPv6 clients or a malformed forwarded address, and a row the database refuses is reported** *(Enterprise)* (#4075). The portal had six copies of its client-address extraction. Two stripped the port from `RemoteAddr` with `strings.LastIndex`, which leaves an IPv6 client's `[::1]:54321` as `[::1]`, and all six returned `X-Forwarded-For` and `X-Real-IP` unvalidated. `admin_audit_log.ip_address` is an `inet`, so PostgreSQL refused the INSERT and the best-effort writer logged a WARNING while the handler returned its correct status. `AUTH_SUCCESS`, `AUTH_FAILURE`, `CREATE_ORG`, `DELETE_ORG` and the self-service reset rows from an IPv6 client were lost (13 in one run of `runtime-e2e/2628`); a malformed forwarded header lost the same rows from any client and made `POST /api/v1/auth/login` answer 500 on its `user_sessions` INSERT. `PASSWORD_CHANGED` rows survived only because every change-password request in that suite carried a valid `X-Forwarded-For`. `audit.ClientIP` (`ee/platform/customer-portal/audit`) now replaces all six: the same sources in the same order, a canonical address, and nothing - NULL, never a proxy's address - for a present header that does not parse. Every INSERT into an `ip_address` column binds it through `audit.NullIP`: `admin_audit_log`, `user_sessions` from the password, SAML and OIDC logins, `sso_login_attempts` and `scim_audit_log`. The swallowing writers of `admin_audit_log`, `config_audit_log`, `scim_audit_log` and the SAML and OIDC `sso_login_attempts` report a lost row as one `ERROR` line carrying `event=audit_row_lost`, the table and the SQLSTATE, so a loss can be counted; a failed write still never fails the request. The connector and LLM-provider handlers' duplicated `config_audit_log` writers call the shared one. Two censuses in that package fail a new write that binds a raw address or a writer that swallows a lost row. `middleware.TestGetClientIP` asserted `[::1]` for an IPv6 `RemoteAddr` - the defect as the contract; it is replaced by tests of the shared function, a real `[::1]` listener through the admin middleware into a real `admin_audit_log`, and the writer against migration 113's table.

- **Security: the customer portal's change-password changes only the signed-in organization's password, and a failed attempt no longer says why** *(Enterprise)* (#4055). `POST /api/v1/auth/change-password` was registered with no session check and took the organization whose password it changed from the `X-Org-ID` header, falling back to an `org_id` route variable. Anyone who knew an org_id - the portal login username, not a secret - could change that organization's password given its current one, and could guess at it: the route answered `404` for no active organization, `400` for no password set and `401` for a wrong password. The route now sits behind the portal's session middleware, the same one every `/api/v1` route uses, and the handler takes the organization from the session alone; nothing in the request can name another one, and a request with no session is refused before any read. No active organization, no password set and a wrong current password all answer the same `401` and body after the same single bcrypt comparison - against a cost-10 placeholder when there is no stored hash, shared with the login handler, which already did this - and differ only in the audit row. Attempts are limited to 5 a minute per client address and, because that key is one a caller can influence, 5 a minute per organization. Every refused attempt is a failed `PASSWORD_CHANGED` row in `admin_audit_log`: the session's organization with the reason, or, with no session, a NULL organization with the organization the request claimed kept in `details.claimed_org_id` as caller-supplied, unverified evidence that is never echoed or used. **Client note:** a caller that sent only `X-Org-ID` now gets `401`; send the `axonflow_session` cookie from `POST /api/v1/auth/login`. No first-party client did. The contract is documented in `docs/enterprise/customer-portal-access.md` and the portal API references under `ee/docs/`. `api/org_scope_test.go`'s scope guard now also matches the `X-Org-ID` header: it matched only query and form spellings, which is how this read went unseen.

- **The customer portal's typed-authoring dry run activates `decide` with the Decision API's delivery, as the agent's decide seam does** *(Enterprise)* (#4046). The shipped corpus no longer binds a mandatory obligation on `decide`, so no activation depends on it today; it keeps the dry run's result equal to the seam's on the day a control binds one.

- **Security: the customer portal's typed-authoring workspace signs the system root with a key of its own, and its activation dry run no longer authorizes the organization's key under the system root** *(Enterprise)* (#4047). `ee/platform/customer-portal/api/typed_authoring.go` passed the workspace's own signing key to activation as the system key - on the surface whose artifacts persist - and activation wrote that key into the trust store the workspace verifies against. The workspace now mints a separate system key for `authoring.SystemAuthority`, activation reads the organization's key without writing anything, and the workspace's own key presented as the system key is refused by name (`SYSTEM_KEY_IS_AN_ORGANIZATION_KEY`). The authority, the durable-store refusal and `migrations/core/178` are the Community entry of the same name above.

- **`axonflow-policy-import --collapse-superseded` removes only what the supersession ledger permits** *(Enterprise)* (#3323). It used to drop whichever generation of a superseded pair lost a strength comparison. On the five live pairs that is the canonical row, and neither generation's pattern contains the other's: no engine adds `(?i)` to a stored pattern, so after a collapse `drop_table_prevention`'s `drop\s+table` was the only DROP TABLE detector in the imported document and `DROP TABLE users` matched nothing. The collapse now removes only the pre-canonical generation of a pair the ledger decides `drop_superseded`, and never a superseder. A capture in which that row still enforces more than one of its superseders is reported as `ledger_decision_contradicts_capture` and the row is kept, as it is when any pair it takes part in cannot be ranked, is ambiguous or is missing a half. No live pair is `drop_superseded`, so on today's ledger the flag removes nothing. The importer reads the ledger through the registry's parser, which refuses a padded `superseded_by` member such as `a, b`.

- **The policy editor shows the platform's own controls, read-only, with each control's assurance class** *(Enterprise)* (#3884). The portal serves `GET /api/v1/typed-policies/system` behind a session and the organization's typed-authoring flag, like every read beside it, and the policy-authoring route gains a Platform controls panel: counts per class, the controls grouped by class with what each class means, and the corpus digest, with no edit, delete or publish control. A control that reaches the page without a class is shown as unclassified, never folded into a default.
- **The customer portal and the policy importer follow #3961: no environment variable sets a detection action** *(Enterprise)* (#3961).
  - **Unified policies API:** `posture_lever` is replaced by `detection_override_category` (`pii`, `sqli`, `dangerous_command` or empty). The Policies page states a row's action and names the organization override that could replace it, instead of striking the action through, because nothing displaces it until an organization records an override. The Detection Posture page's default is now "Default (policy action)".
  - **`axonflow-policy-import -posture LEVER=action`** is kept, and authors the action into the imported documents on the categories that variable reached before v11. That table moved into the importer from `platform/decision/legacycompile`, whose `legacy_posture_levers.tsv` and the registry's `detection_posture_fold.tsv` are removed.
  - **AWS Marketplace template:** the `SQLIAction`, `PIIAction`, `SensitiveDataAction` and `DangerousQueryAction` parameters and their container environment are removed. A stack update that still passes them fails validation; drop them.

- **The enterprise half of the decide plane's enforcing seam: the portal and the policy importer read the moved deployment vocabulary, and the organization-settings reader's test now asserts a stored `enforce` is READ** (#3895 PR-A2, #4011). `ee/platform/customer-portal/api/typed_authoring.go` and `ee/platform/policy/cmd/axonflow-policy-import/main.go` import `platform/shared/authoringvocabulary` for the licence-free vocabulary; edition resolution is still `authoringedition.Resolve`, so nothing a caller observes changes. `TestOrgSettingsReaderRefusesAStoredEnforceOnTheDecisionAxis` (`platform/shared/identity/compat_org_settings_test.go`, `//go:build enterprise`) asserted the refusal #4000 removed, and reddened only on the enterprise-tagged unit lane, which had been dark; it is renamed `TestOrgSettingsReaderReadsAStoredEnforceOnTheDecisionAxis`, with its two entries in `platform/shared/identity/compatmutation/mutation_gate_test.go`. The ADR-065 amendment in `technical-docs/architecture-decisions/ADR-065-policy-decision-and-identity-control-plane.md` records category admission as the plane restriction's third arm, with the per-plane counts appended.

- **The legacy policy importer reported an action the deployment does not enforce on the two planes the detection posture cannot reach, and with `--collapse-superseded` that dropped the STRONGER generation of a superseded pair** (follow-up to #3962). `BuildPlan` applied `Posture.Apply` unconditionally to `PlaneResult.ResolvedAction` - a field whose own documentation says it is the value before the lever - while the compiler applies the lever only where `PlaneSpec.PostureLever` (renamed `PlaneSpec.PassesOrgOverrides` by #3961) is true. It is FALSE on `proxy_tier` (a plane #4253 later removed), whose engine resolves through `StaticPolicyRepository.GetEffective` and never sees the override map, and on `cowork_ingest`, whose coercion is carried by `PlaneSpec.ForcedAction` instead and which the planner ignored entirely. Driven on the plane the CLI's own usage example names: under `-posture SQLI_ACTION=block`, `drop_table_prevention` (block) and `sys_sqli_drop_table` (warn) both reported `block`, ranked equal, and a collapse then dropped a row on an equality that does not exist in that deployment - the silent enforcement downgrade this package's own doc comment says it exists to prevent. The planner now reads `EnforcedAction` and re-derives nothing.

  **A reported-disposition change ships with it.** A plane-scoped import no longer inherits a defect earned on a plane it is not importing: `outcomeFor` reads `Record.StatusForPlane(plane)` rather than the row-level `Record.Status`, so a row stops being reported as `imported_with_preserved_defect` because the posture displaced an action on `decide`, `gateway` or `mcp` while the import was planning `proxy_tier` (a plane `-plane` refuses since #4253). The row-level status is unchanged and still sees every plane. Measured across two compilations of one row differing ONLY in `Posture`: the resolved action, the emitted policy and the supersession winner were identical, and the status was the only thing that moved.

- **The per-organization decision mode may hold `enforce`** *(Enterprise)* (#3895, migration `enterprise/156`). Migration 150 wrote `CHECK (... IN ('off','shadow'))` and said why: "the ADR-065 decision plane becomes an authority at v11". This is v11. The operator's cutover ruling makes the anchored engine the enforcer and the legacy engine the **recorded opt-out** until v12 removes it, so the value 150 refused is the value the axis may now hold. `NULL` still means "no per-org record; the process value decides". **The process default is NOT moved by this change** - it ships as `off` until a plane has an enforcing seam, for the reason the Community entry above gives - so this column becoming writable does not by itself change which engine decides. Once a plane does enforce, a row holding `shadow` or `off` is an organization **opted out**, which is the no-redeploy rollback lever.

  **The down migration is deliberately not symmetric.** Re-adding 150's narrower CHECK against a table containing `enforce` FAILS, because the ALTER validates existing rows - a rollback that works only on deployments that never used the feature. So rows are rewritten `enforce` -> `shadow` FIRST, and the migration **counts and names the organizations** it is about to move off the anchored engine, because that is a behaviour change on live traffic and an operator must see it happen rather than infer it from a metric afterwards.

- **Three operator rulings recorded as ADR amendments, so the next lane inherits a decision rather than a question** (#3961, #3968, #3975, #3880). **ADR-065**: a detector's implementation does not vary by plane — the 2026-09-07 "proxy_tier runs bare" fact is retired by #3965, and the shared engine's own request/response divergence (#3968, a Luhn-valid card behind an invalid one, invisible on one path and visible on the other) is now implementation work under that rule rather than a design question; and the four detection environment variables (`PII_ACTION`, `SQLI_ACTION`, `DANGEROUS_COMMAND_ACTION`, `SENSITIVE_DATA_ACTION`) are removed as action-setters in v11, the stored action winning automatically and the change announced in release notes, migration notes and the startup log rather than by refusing to boot. **ADR-066**: durable typed-policy storage is edition-neutral — *gate the constructs, not the persistence* — so Community gets the typed-policy tables in the core schema while org-root authoring, group scope, separation of duties and the legacy importer stay Enterprise, with the guard required to be derived rather than hand-listed and proved on the tree `simulate-community-mirror.sh` actually stages; and the Community ceiling stays policy-counted at 20 (first 20 in the existing order, or a clean refusal). Each amendment names the measurement it rests on: the ADR-066 one was decided on a booted Community stack where publish → activate → restart → `404 nothing_active` while the legacy rows survived.
- **Five RBI compliance routes were registered on the production router and answered `405` to every request, so there was no way to update an RBI FREE-AI AI system, model validation or incident, and no way to resolve one** (#3935). The mux registered `PUT`; the handlers implement `PATCH`; `PATCH` was registered nowhere. `POST /api/v1/rbi/incidents/{id}/resolve` had no case in its handler's sub-route switch at all. Every one of these had been unreachable since the module's first release, on the surface an Indian banking regulator reads.

  **The correction went to the REGISTRATION, not to the handlers.** The router now registers the verb each handler implements - `PATCH` on `/api/v1/rbi/ai-systems/{id}`, `/validations/{id}` and `/incidents/{id}` - and `/resolve` is served. Changing the handlers to answer `PUT` would have been fixing the evidence. `PUT /api/v1/rbi/reports/{id}` is removed rather than repointed, because there is no update-report operation on that path under any verb; a board report's mutations are `/submit`, `/approve` and `/reject`. **This is a wire change for anyone who wrote against the old document: the update verb is `PATCH`.** No client can have depended on the old one - it returned 405 - but the verb in `docs/api/orchestrator-api.yaml`, `docs/compliance/rbi-free-ai.md` and `ee/docs/api/rbi-api.md` has changed and all three are updated. `POST /incidents/{id}/resolve` requires a non-empty `resolution`: it is the only writer of `resolution_summary` on an incident record, so an incident resolved without one could never acquire it afterwards.

  **#3935 said four routes and there were five, and the fifth is the one that mattered most.** `PUT /api/v1/rbi/ai-systems/{id}` was registered AND published in `docs/api/orchestrator-api.yaml` - so the document and the router agreed with each other, both disagreed with the handler, and BOTH directions of the route-parity guard added in #3949 were green while the published contract promised an operation that answered 405 to every caller. The four the issue listed were found only because they happened to be undocumented. **Both parity directions compare the SPEC to the REGISTRATION; nothing compared the REGISTRATION to the HANDLER, and that is where this entire class lives.**

  So the durable half of this change is a guard that asks the question no existing instrument could: `platform/orchestrator/rbi/wire_registered_verbs_are_served_test.go` builds the module, registers it through the production registrar, **walks the router for its own population** and DRIVES every registered verb of every registered route, failing on a 405. Nothing is read from source and nothing is listed by hand, so it cannot be blind to a spelling. Run for the first time it reported the `ai-systems` verb and **three more nobody had filed**: `OPTIONS` on all three `/api/v1/rbi/policies/*` routes answered 405, because their method check was `!= GET` - so the CORS preflight of every cross-origin read of an RBI policy template was refused and the browser never sent the `GET`.
