Those three also emitted `text/plain` through `http.Error` against a contract whose every response declares `application/json` (the #3941 / #3949 envelope class); they use the module's own writers now.

  The four routes on the issue are each driven end to end through the production registrar, and the assertion is a **read-back of the changed field**, never a status code: "not 405" is satisfied by a handler that accepts a request and writes nothing. For that read-back to mean anything the store needs DB semantics - this package's in-memory repositories hand out the stored pointer, so a service that mutated a record and never called `Update` would still read back the new value - so the repositories are wrapped to copy on `Get` and on `Update`, and a control cuts the write and requires the read-back to notice. Every assertion here is mutation-proved with the mutation verified PRESENT before its red is believed.

  The four `undocumentedRouteAllowances()` rows holding these routes named a revisit condition that was a named observable, and it fired exactly as written: registering the implemented verb made all four match nothing and the guard's own stale-allowance ratchet reported each by name. They are deleted. The `/resolve` row in `api-spec-coverage-baseline.tsv` goes with them, and that file's header note - which recorded that documenting `GET` on a path-keyed row retired the evidence about the `PUT` on the same path - is kept and extended, because the shape recurs.

  **Proved against a live stack, not only in unit tests.** `runtime-e2e/3066_rbi_org_scope` gains seven assertions on this second property of the same surface — it already boots the one thing they need and nothing else in CI does, a live orchestrator with the RBI module wired and `migrations/industry/banking/301` applied. Every update assertion reads the ROW back with `psql`. Four of the seven were **measured** failing against the pre-fix revision of `wire.go` and `incident_handlers.go`; the other three (two fixture controls and PUT-is-405) pass either way and are labelled as such in the script rather than counted as pre-fix failures.

  A third pre-existing ratchet caught this branch and is recorded here rather than in a PR body nobody reopens: the customer portal's `TestEveryOrchestratorRouteIsClassifiedForTheProxy` (#3130) reported the three new `PATCH` routes as unclassified AND four `PUT` rows in `proxyRefusedOrchestratorRoutes` as stale. The refusal rows move to the verbs that now exist; `PUT /api/v1/rbi/reports/{id}` is deleted because no route is there any more. The portal's own posture is unchanged - RBI writes stay refused through the portal proxy, which is what those rows have always said.

  **Not done, and filed rather than left implicit (#3954):** three `delete*` handlers and `POST /incidents/{id}/status` are implemented and registered on no route. They are the mirror image of this defect and the new guard **cannot** see them - an unregistered handler verb answers 404, not 405. Registering three destructive verbs on a regulated compliance surface is a retention decision, not a routing fix, and the tree is currently inconsistent about it: `DELETE /api/v1/rbi/ai-systems/{id}` is registered and documented while its three siblings are not.
- **Typed authoring has a durable store, and the policies a deployment already has can be moved into it** (#3776, epic #3549, ADR-065). `authoring.Store` keeps every rule it had - re-verification against the trust store, separation of author and approver duties, the version advance, the parent chain - and storage moves behind an `authoring.Backend` interface. The in-process backend stays the default, so a deployment that has not applied `migrations/enterprise/155` behaves exactly as before. **The edition and the backend are independent axes**: the edition decides which constructs may be written, the backend decides where what was written is kept, and a Community deployment with a durable store is a coherent thing. Two properties changed in the seam because a durable store cannot be trusted to reinvent them: the ACTIVE version is now DERIVED from the activation history rather than stored beside it, which removes a second record of one fact, and `AppendActivation` takes the parent the caller checked against and refuses when the tip has moved - a mutex is atomic in one process, and two portal replicas can both read active digest D, both find their candidate's parent is D, and both write. `migrations/enterprise/155` gives the three tables FORCE row-level security with strict org equality, append-only triggers that bind the OWNER where a privilege revoke cannot, and a column-narrow `GRANT UPDATE (revoked_at, revoked_reason)` for the one legitimate mutation. **The importer presents BOTH generations of a superseded pair and defaults to the stronger action**, because #3323's five superseded rows are each STRONGER than what replaced them - migration 067 relaxed them by category and by an explicit `sys_pii_*` id list - so an import that silently kept the newer of a pair would weaken enforcement while reporting success. It is a dry run by default, idempotent on the document SOURCE digest, and refuses to decide what an operator must: a divergent pair is reported by name rather than resolved. **`-edition` is required and not defaulted**, for the reason `authoring.NewAPI` gives about its own positional argument - the deployment most likely to run an import is the one migrating off the legacy model, and defaulting to enterprise would let a Community deployment publish constructs it cannot author and will be refused on next edit.

  **The legacy write freeze is NOT in this change.** `migrations/core/172` makes `static_policies` and `dynamic_policies` SELECT-only to the application roles, and it ships separately under a standing ruling: it does not land until the importer is demonstrated usable on a real Community database. The authoring half exists, so a deployment can write a NEW typed policy; until the import is demonstrated it cannot necessarily move the ones it already has, and freezing the legacy path in that state removes the only thing that works. Nothing here should be read as "the legacy tables are read-only".

- **The customer portal's task definition and compose service now receive `AXONFLOW_LICENSE_KEY`** *(Enterprise)* — the Enterprise half of the fix above. `CustomerPortalTaskDefinition` reads it from the same `LicenseKeySecret` through the same `TaskExecutionRole` that already serves `AgentTaskDefinition` and `OrchestratorTaskDefinition`, so this is a missing entry rather than a missing IAM grant and no new permission ships. The portal also rebuilds an organization's authoring plane when the deployment's boundary changes under a cached workspace, which the orchestrator route has done since it was written and this surface did not: a licence that expired mid-process left the Enterprise construct set in force here until somebody restarted the container, while the orchestrator narrowed at the next publication. The comparison is over the whole boundary and not the edition alone, because a lapsing licence moves the tier from established to unestablished while the edition it folds to stays `community` — comparing editions would see no change and keep a store built without the duty rule.


- **The customer portal reads its authoring edition from the verified licence rather than from the build tag it carries** (#3907). `//go:build enterprise` says which code was compiled, not which licence the deployment holds, and an Evaluation deployment runs the same image — so reading the edition off the tag would have given the portal the Enterprise construct set while the community route, which reads the licence, refused the same document: one deployment, two answers to what may be published, decided by which door was used. `tier_limits.go` in `platform/agent/license` states the rule the other way round and this now obeys it: the deployment mode "may narrow what a build registers, it never grants a limit". The portal also delegates catalog resolution to the shared `authoringcatalog` package instead of holding its own copy of the switch and the realm-attribute map. No behaviour change for an Enterprise-licensed deployment: its constructs and its separation-of-duties requirement are byte-for-byte what they were, which the library's pre-existing publication tests assert by running unmodified.

- **Two probes in the twelve-plane decision-shadow canary could never evaluate, so it paged `dev@` every five to ten minutes with a coverage failure no operator could act on** (#3602). Five consecutive runs on `try.getaxonflow.com` reported `failed_step: coverage` naming `map`, `openai_compatible` and `wcp`, while every other probe returned 200 with `evaluated: true`. Two independent defects, one per probe.

  **The `openai` probe sent a hard-coded placeholder key.** The argument for the placeholder was that a blocked payload is refused at the policy gate (`openai_compat_handler.go:433`) before the key is attached as a Bearer token at `:450`, so it is never transmitted. True, and conditional on the payload being blocked: this stack blocks none of the corpus, so every probe took the `:450` path and the provider answered `401 invalid_api_key`. The key now comes from a new optional parameter, `DecisionShadowProviderKeySecretArn`. Left empty, the probe is **skipped** with the reason and the parameter name in the report, and `openai_compatible` leaves the coverage denominator instead of failing it forever. Set, the probe runs; and a configured secret that is unreadable or empty **fails the run** with `failed_step: read-provider-key` rather than degrading to the skip, because the skip predicate is keyed on the ARN (the configuration) and not on the key value. **An operator who wants this plane probed must supply that ARN**; nothing in this change mints a key.

  **The `plan_execute` probe omitted `plan_id`, which starves BOTH `wcp` and `map`.** `/api/v1/plan/execute` executes a STORED plan: `executePlanHandler` reads `context.plan_id`, refuses without one at `platform/orchestrator/run.go:4906`, retrieves the row at `:4941`, and only then evaluates at `:5032` over `plan.Query` - the query on the PLAN, not on the execute request. The probe sent `context: {steps: [...]}` and no id, so it was refused 126 lines before the wcp evaluator on every run; the agent wrapped that 400 into an HTTP 200 carrying `error` AND the proxy plane's `policy_info`, which is why it read as a healthy response with an application error rather than as a dead probe. The probe now mints a plan first (`request_type: multi-agent-plan`, which unlike `generate-plan` reaches the block at `agent/run.go:2972` that lifts `plan_id` to the top level) and executes THAT id. **The generate call's response is never scored as evidence**: it is evaluated by the proxy planes, and returning it verbatim would credit `wcp` and `map` with an evaluation neither performed. A 429 on it is the one pass-through, so the run's rate-limited exit still fires.

  **This fixes `wcp`, and `map` needs one more thing that is not in this repository's control.** Reaching the execute route is necessary for both planes and sufficient only for `wcp`: `map`'s single call site sits behind `AXONFLOW_HITL_ENABLED`, which no deploy surface here sets. That is #3886's subject and is not restated here - what this change removes is the other cause, the one that stopped `wcp` and `map` being reached by the canary at all. Until the posture changes, `map` can appear only in `planes_inferred_only`, never in `planes_covered`.

  **One predicate now decides both what runs and what coverage demands.** The edition test was written out three times - once for the denominator and twice in the run loop - and a plane demanded by one copy and unreachable by another fails coverage on every run with no remedy, which is what defect A produced. `_skip_reason` is the single answer, and it also builds `planes_skipped` - a sixth `planes_*` field carried by all three report shapes through the same single builder #3555 introduced for the other five - so a run covering ten planes and skipping two no longer reads identically to one covering twelve.

  `tests/regression-test-required/decision_shadow_canary_probe_preconditions_test.sh` drives the real probes lifted from the template: it reads the `plan_id` requirement out of `run.go` rather than remembering it, refuses a probe that ships a credential the source itself marks non-functional (scanning STRING LITERALS through the AST, because an absence check that greps text is defeated by the comment explaining the rule - which it was, on its first run), and holds every rule to a mutant broken in that rule's dimension, asserting the exact SET of rows each mutant reds. It SKIPS on a community checkout, where `infrastructure/` does not exist, and FAILS if `ee/` is present, so it cannot pass vacuously in the tree it is meant to bite. `decision_shadow_canary_evidence_test.sh` is driven against the two-request probe and the skip path, and its plane-set expectations are read from `_skip_reason` rather than from `PLANE_MAP` alone, so a skipped plane is not reported as one that vanished.
- **The customer portal UI moves to Next.js 16.3.4 and sharp 0.35.4, closing an unauthenticated remote code execution** (CVE-2026-75604 / GHSA-2xp9-vwfh-vxw4, CRITICAL, in Next.js Image Optimization; and GHSA-rgj7-g3m4-5g8c, HIGH, sharp via libheif). **THE DECLARED RANGE WAS NOT THE VULNERABLE THING - THE LOCKFILE WAS**: `package.json` already read `^16.2.11`, which permits 16.3.3, while `package-lock.json` pinned 16.2.11, so the fix is the resolved install and the range bump only stops a future resolve landing below it. `sharp` is not a direct dependency at all; it is pinned through `overrides`, which is where it had to be raised. The floor is `^16.3.3` (the first fixed release) and the lockfile resolves 16.3.4, the current 16.x patch. `ee/platform/clients/banking-demo` carries a second Next.js surface that no advisory named and that is built by `build-client-images.yml`; its floor moves from `^16.2.0` to `^16.3.3` as well. It has no lockfile, so a fresh install there already resolved above the fix - the change makes that explicit rather than leaving it to the resolver.

- **Two of the six SEBI readiness pillars queried relations that no migration creates, so they answered "could not verify" on every deployment in the world and understated customers whose controls were demonstrably working** (#3874). The SEBI AI/ML readiness pack is a document an Indian securities regulator reads. On production-US banking-demo it scored 40%, with `PII Detection Policies` and `Retention Configuration` Unknown and `Human Oversight` Warning, on a tenant whose PAN/Aadhaar redaction was enforcing and verified the same morning.

  **Two pillars queried relations that no migration creates.** `checkPIIPolicies` read `policies` and `checkHITLConfiguration` read `hitl_config`; zero `CREATE TABLE` statements in `migrations/` name either, so the undefined-relation branch was not a defensive corner but the ONLY branch either ever took. They now read `static_policies` and `hitl_approval_queue`. The scope key was wrong too, and would have stayed wrong under a repoint alone: the old predicate was `tenant_id = $1` while the value the readiness path is handed is the ORG key, and on `static_policies` those are different axes - `org_id` is the tenancy boundary `core/165` made NOT NULL, `tenant_id` defaults to `'global'` and every seeded policy carries exactly that.

  **The third pillar was investigated and its code deliberately left alone.** The issue listed `checkRetentionCompliance` beside the other two; it does not share the defect, because `audit_retention_config` exists (`core/026`). The real finding is that **nothing in the product ever writes a row to it** - every `INSERT` in the tree is in a test - so its "could not verify" is not one tenant's state but every deployment's, permanently, with no operator action able to change it. It is right to say so, and it now says why: a long note on the function records what was found, that a draft made the pillar resolve the period in force through `get_effective_retention_days` instead, and the two reasons that draft was reverted rather than shipped. First, it contradicted this file's own settled position - `getRetentionConfig`, 350 lines away, was changed by #3435 to STOP treating that default as evidence, so the readiness half would have rendered a confident PASS beside a retention endpoint reporting the same five data types `not_available`. Second, `audit_retention_defaults` is a global CROSS-REGULATOR vocabulary: `enterprise/139` seeds US presets correctly BELOW the SEBI floor (`reg_b_adverse_action_records` at 760 days, `nydfs_cybersecurity_audit_trail` at 1095) and its own header says it put them there *because* the SEBI check did not read that table. Measured on a live enterprise stack carrying 12 default rows, the draft failed the pillar naming both US regulations. Making this pillar answerable needs the retention configuration surface that does not exist, with both halves of the pack moving together; filed, not ridden on a bug fix.

  **The fail-closed contract is unchanged, and that is the point.** A previous revision returned `true` on the undefined-relation branch, so the pack asserted PAN and Aadhaar detection to a regulator on the strength of a query against a relation that has never existed (#3435). Every pillar still refuses when it cannot read, proven against a real Postgres 42P01 rather than a hand-written error string. `checkHITLConfiguration` gained the third `(ok, verified, details)` answer its two siblings already had; until now a deployment nobody could inspect reported identically to one measured to have no oversight.

  **The PII predicate matches what a policy DETECTS, not what it is called.** `name ILIKE '%pan%'` matched "company panel"; the obvious replacement, `category = 'pii_detection'`, is a generic bucket that also holds US SSN, credit-card, UPI, GSTIN, passport, voter-ID and PIN-code detectors, so it would have let a US-SSN policy evidence a SEBI control. It reads `category = 'pii-india'` (the system tier) or `metadata->>'pii_type' IN ('pan_number','aadhaar_number')` (the industry-template tier), and the policy scope predicate is copied from `PolicyLoader.loadFromDatabase` - the code that actually enforces - so the pillar cannot report a posture the gateway does not apply.

  **`static_policies` is row-level-security enabled, and the way that was nearly missed is the reusable part.** A first draft read it unwrapped, on the strength of a grep for literal `ALTER TABLE ... ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY` statements *run with a positive control that passed*. `core/018` enables it from inside a `DO` block via `EXECUTE format(...)`, which no such grep could ever see - the control proved only that the grep could find the statements it was able to find. Under `axonflow_app_role`, the NOBYPASSRLS pool that has been the default since v9.0.0, both scope passes matched zero rows and the pillars returned a confident MEASURED negative telling an operator to seed policies `core/031` already seeded. Every policy read is now wrapped, and `TestRealPG_PillarsMeasureUnderTheAppRole` asserts `pg_class.relrowsecurity` - the running database, not the migration text - before measuring anything through it.

  The wire contract is unchanged - `SEBIComplianceCheck.status` already carried `unknown` in its enum - but its description in **`docs/api/orchestrator-api.yaml`** said "two of the five checks assign it" and cited the missing `policies` relation, both now stale; it is rewritten there, including why `unknown` blocks `ready` for two pillars and not for Human Oversight. That file is the one path in this entry that reaches the community mirror; everything else is `//go:build enterprise` source the sync strips.

  Proven in the Real-PG lane rather than asserted: the stock Aadhaar detector IS counted, the stock US-SSN detector in the generic bucket is NOT, a soft-deleted policy is not a live control, the pillars measure identically under the app-role and superuser pools, and the approval-queue read returns rows under `axonflow_app_role` only because of its `withOrgScope` wrap. Twenty-one mutations of the predicates, the wraps, the guards and the fail-closed branches were each confirmed to fail a test - and three of them did not kill on the first attempt, each time because of a defect in the test rather than in the code, including a refusal assertion that sqlmock satisfied by itself until it was made to assert the REASON for the refusal. A relation census over the readiness surface re-derives the queried-relation list from source at test time, so a pillar added later against a phantom relation is caught on its first run.

- **The v3-certificate-at-a-v2-verifier direction is now pinned by a golden fixture instead of reasoned about in prose** (#3719). `RUNBOOK_DECISION_PROOF_KEY_ROTATION.md` §5.2 tells an operator mid-upgrade which refusal means which half of the fleet is behind; one direction was pinned by a test and the other was reasoning, and its earlier draft had named the wrong reason for the case an operator meets first. `platform/shared/requirements/proof/testdata/v3_certificate_at_v2_verifier.json` now carries a v3 certificate minted by this tree and the verdict the **v10.3.0** verifier (`ec09d2a91`, the last release that computes v2 signed bytes - v10.4.0 already carries v3) gave it: `certificate_signature_invalid`, which confirms the runbook's reasoning. The verdict is produced by the old verifier through a harness compiled against that tag, never by this tree simulating it; `scripts/ci/regenerate-v3-at-v2-fixture.sh` reproduces both halves, and the pin test also parses §5.2's table so the runbook and the observation cannot drift apart.

- **`marketplace.GetUsageHistory` returned an error on every call, and no test had ever reached it** (#3699). The query interpolated a placeholder inside a SQL string literal (`INTERVAL '$1 days'`), which Postgres reads as literal text, so the statement required zero parameters and the driver refused the call with *"got 1 parameters but the statement requires 0"*. Fixed to `make_interval(days => $1)` in both the `platform` and `ee` copies. It was never observed because the only test that reaches it is gated on `DATABASE_URL`, and no job set one for this package: the arm selected ee packages by name, and the arm that did run it supplied `TEST_PG_INTEGRATION` without a database URL. The derived arm sets both, so the test executed for the first time and failed - the argument for this change made by the code rather than about it. WHICH copy it executed is a separate fact and not a comfortable one: that test lives in `ee/platform/agent/marketplace/` but imports the `platform` twin, while the enterprise image overlays the `ee` copy over the `platform` one, so the copy that ships is covered only by an sqlmock test that never parses SQL. Both copies are fixed; the coverage gap is recorded and tracked on #3820.
- **A test that sits beside one copy of a forked package and imports the other is now a declared exception rather than an accident** (#3699). `ee/platform/testcensus` walks every `*_test.go` under the root `ee` module and flags an EXTERNAL test package under `ee/platform/X` that imports `axonflow/platform/X`, because that binds its subject to the twin of the package it sits beside - and where the enterprise image overlays the `ee` copy onto the `platform` one, the file that ships is then the file nothing ran. An in-package test importing the twin for shared types is a different thing and is not flagged; the classifier is exercised on both, so the distinction cannot quietly erode. One row is declared today, with its reason and its tracking issue.
- **`ee/platform/connectors/amadeus` unit tests no longer resolve the official Amadeus hosts over live DNS** (#3699). A package-level resolver, stubbed in `TestMain` to a routable public address for the two official hosts and refusing every other name, feeds the SSRF pre-flight; a control asserts a private answer is still refused. Twelve subtests failed wherever DNS was unavailable, and the package was one resolver outage from failing a required lane once the derived arm put it on one.
- **The twelve-plane canary could not pass on any run, and one refused plane zeroed the other eleven** (#3602). The `openai_compatible` probe sent no `X-Provider-Key`, so `/v1/chat/completions` refused it at the presence check *before* any evaluation on every payload — and because the run ended on the first unevaluated probe, no plane recorded evidence, every five minutes, into the alert topic.

  **Two defects, and a text fix would have shipped the second.** The probe now sends a syntactically valid, deliberately non-functional key — the check is presence-only, and a blocked payload returns before the upstream request is built, so on the payloads this plane is scored on the key is never transmitted anywhere. And the evidence predicate now reads the error **code**: a policy denial on that route is HTTP 400 with `policy_denied`, the same status the same handler uses for `missing_provider_key`, so the plane's strongest evidence and its weakest were indistinguishable by status alone.

  A failing plane is now recorded **per plane** and the run continues. The coverage check already refused to pass a plane that produced nothing, so failing fast bought no loudness and cost every other plane its evidence.

  The argument for why a non-functional key is honest evidence — and why an allow-shaped payload's upstream failure is deliberately *not* counted — is in `docs/operations/decision-shadow-canary.md`, where this template's header already says the full argument lives. `tests/regression-test-required/decision_shadow_canary_evidence_test.sh` drives the real predicate lifted from the template against the response shapes measured on the live stack, and drives the probe itself to prove the header is sent: its first version searched the source for the header name and was satisfied by the comment explaining it.

- **The base canary's MCP step now authenticates, stopping an hourly false alarm the rewrite introduced** (#3602). Rewriting step 2 to call a method the dispatcher actually implements moved the request behind the auth gate: an UNKNOWN JSON-RPC method reaches method-not-found and is served HTTP 200, while a KNOWN one is refused at the auth layer first. So `initialize` began returning `401 Registration required` against production every hour. It now sends the credentials step 1 mints, exactly as the audit-search step does.

  Measured against the live stack rather than reasoned about: `initialize` unauthenticated 401; `initialize` with `params.context.tenant_id` **also** 401, so the unauth path's tenant-resolution route is not the fix and was tried; `mcpCheckInput` with `context.tenant_id` 200 with `method not found`; `ping` unauthenticated 401. The third of those is the original defect reproduced in production — the step passing hourly while dispatching nothing — and is why it was rewritten at all.

  Pinned by a row in `tests/regression-test-required/synthetic_monitoring_two_stacks_test.sh`, which asserts the step-2 request carries the credentials and refuses an extraction that runs past it into the audit-search call below — that call also passes `basic_auth`, so a sloppy extraction would be satisfied by the wrong request's credentials.

- **The twelve-plane decision-shadow canary, and the base canary that had been failing hourly against production-US** (#3602, epic #3555). ADR-065 gate 18 is stated PER PLANE and needs a non-vacuous denominator on each one; measured on the house stacks 2026-09-06T20:26Z..2026-09-07T13:29Z, community-SaaS produced comparisons on five of twelve planes, production-US produced zero on all twelve, and seven planes have never been observed in production on either. `infrastructure/cloudformation/synthetic-monitoring-decision-shadow.yaml` is a third synthetic-monitoring stack that exercises every implemented plane on a schedule, declares every request synthetic via `X-Axonflow-Synthetic-Probe` so the ADR-065 volume floor is never read off our own probe, mints nothing (it reuses the identity canary's credential, because `registrationIPLimit` is 5/hour/IP and #3655/#3698 record that canary defeating itself on exactly that cap), and never presents `X-Axonflow-PEP-Handshake`, which would RESET the window it exists to fill.

  **The base canary's step 2 was reporting success while evaluating nothing**: it POSTed a JSON-RPC method the dispatcher does not implement, got an error body served with HTTP 200, checked only the status, and passed every hour. Every probe now carries an evidence predicate, and a 403 is a success here because this measures whether an EVALUATION happened, not whether a request succeeded.

  **`DeployBaseCanary` is now `BaseCanaryRequested AND NOT TargetIsEnterprise`.** The community-shaped base canary calls `/api/v1/register`, which no enterprise stack exposes, so it had been firing hourly against production-US for a release. An operator who passes `true` against an enterprise stack now gets no canary rather than a standing false alarm - a missing canary is visible as a missing signal, one that cannot succeed is an alarm everybody learns to mute. `target_edition` gains `auto` and takes it as the default: on a recognised target URL it takes the derivation, on the override path it derives from `env_name_override`, and where nothing can be derived it REFUSES rather than falling back to `community` - which is what a default redeploy of production-US used to do, re-enabling the canary with every input at its default.

  The design argument lives in `docs/operations/decision-shadow-canary.md` rather than the template header, because that template runs close to the 51,200-byte `--template-body` cap the deploy uses and an argument shortened to fit a deploy limit belongs somewhere it can be read. That page ships to the community mirror, as do the corpus tests in `platform/decision/legacycompile/` that keep the canary's request shapes honest against the seeded policy rows - the probe shapes are derived from the shared conformance corpus, not invented for the canary.

- **ADR-065 states the detector CRUD boundary** (#3786). A dated amendment to the "Inspection and risk" section records the two platform-versioned implementation classes, what an enterprise operator may configure on a shipped detector (enable/disable, emit, obligations, threshold, scope) and what is versioned code at every edition (a pattern's text, an algorithm's internals, and the entry's class, version, conformance and edition); that "delete" means disable; that the Community/Enterprise split is an edition gate on the authoring route rather than a second policy model; and that Phase 5 retires the legacy decision machinery while keeping every detector implementation. `technical-docs/designs/DETECTOR_REGISTRY_DESIGN.md` is the design behind it, including the reuse census against the action registry and the plugin/gateway reader table. **Design only: no runtime behaviour changes.**

- **The decision-shadow recording rules and alerts that read the new label** (#3817). `platform/monitoring/` is excluded from the community sync, so this half does not ship in the mirror even though the counters it reads do - a distinction an earlier draft of this entry got wrong, and the same wrong belief put two rule-file tests in a mirrored package where they could not find their own input.

  Four recording rules - an organic denominator, a synthetic one, an organically-vacuous verdict and a refused-without-comparison verdict - and two alerts. `AxonFlowDecisionShadowWindowCanaryOnly` (info) fires when a plane's every comparison is our own probe, which is the ordinary state of a quiet stack and the reading a gate-18 sign-off must not mistake for tenant traffic. `AxonFlowDecisionShadowPlaneCannotCompare` (warning) names a plane that is reached, watched, and structurally unable to compare - measured on the v10.4.0 gate (b) run, where `mcp` refused ten of ten observations while its gate-18 numerator read the pre-created zero, byte-identical to watched-and-clean.

  The refused-without-comparison rule suppresses on the ORGANIC comparison count, not the total. Against the total, the twelve-plane canary would have silenced the alert added to describe the defect that canary's own run surfaced.

- **Compliance report generation was OFF on every stack the marketplace template builds, and the failure named a knob that had nowhere to be turned** (#3304). The orchestrator resolves its artifact backend from `AUDIT_EXPORT_*` (`cloudstorage.NewStorageConfigFromEnv`) and `ee/platform/aws-marketplace/cloudformation-ecs-fargate.yaml` set none of them, so every generated report died at the storage stage with *"this deployment has no artifact storage backend configured (set `AUDIT_EXPORT_STORAGE_TYPE` and its bucket/credential variables on the orchestrator)"*. That message names a variable deliberately - it is the one message in `compliancereport/service.go` that does, because it is the single failure a reader can act on immediately - and on this deployment there was nothing to act on.

  The template now provisions a dedicated `ComplianceArtifactsBucket` (Retain, versioned, SSE-KMS, public access blocked, **no expiry rule** - auto-deleting compliance evidence is itself a finding) with its own CMK, grants the orchestrator's task role object-scoped `s3:PutObject`/`GetObject` through a standalone `AWS::IAM::Policy`, and sets `AUDIT_EXPORT_STORAGE_TYPE`, `_S3_BUCKET`, `_S3_REGION`, `_S3_ENCRYPTION` and `_S3_KMS_KEY_ID` on the orchestrator container.

  Three decisions are load bearing and each is written down where it applies. The existing ALB access-log bucket is **not** reusable - it is the ELB log-delivery target, it is SSE-S3 on an exception scoped to "low-sensitivity HTTP request metadata", it expires objects after 90 days, and it is unversioned. A **dedicated** CMK rather than `AxonFlowKMSKey`, because that key protects Secrets Manager and one `TaskRole` is shared by every service in the stack. And the grant is a **standalone policy** rather than an inline statement, because inline it closed a three-resource cycle (`TaskRole` → bucket → key → `TaskRole`) that `cfn-lint` refuses with three `E3004`s and CloudFormation cannot order.

  The variables the template does **not** set matter as much as the ones it does: `cloudstorage/s3.go` installs a static credential provider only when both `AUDIT_EXPORT_S3_ACCESS_KEY` and `_SECRET_KEY` are present, and otherwise resolves the Fargate task role. Setting them - the obvious move, since the compose file does for MinIO - would replace the scoped IAM grant with a long-lived credential embedded in a task definition. A test asserts their **absence**, sliced to the orchestrator's container and matched as `Name`/`Value` pairs rather than as substrings of a 271KB file.
- **Seventeen duplicate files deleted from `ee/platform/agent/`** (#3725). The
  whole of `circuitbreaker` (10), `rbi` (3) and `connectors` (1) were copies of
  the platform files differing only by the `//go:build enterprise` constraint
  the platform copy carries, with no importer anywhere in `ee/`; `hitl/doc.go`
  is documentation with no declarations; and `node_enforcement/alerts.go` plus
  its test exercise only symbols that are code-identical across the pair. The
  surviving platform copies are enterprise-tagged and the image is built with
  that tag, so the shipped binary is unchanged. The remaining 62 pairs are
  recorded, not collapsed: 19 are the same source trapped inside a forked
  package (Go compiles packages, not files), 26 are unintended drift between
  two enterprise-only copies and are filed as #3820-#3825, and 17 are ADR-066
  Decision 5's intended community-stub-against-enterprise-implementation
  pattern, which is not duplication.

- **ADR-066 and PRD section 6 amended for the scale boundaries** (#3593). A dated ADR-066 amendment records the ruled values, the resolution rule (the signed licence, never the deployment mode), the placement rule (restriction code ships to Community, feature code stays under `ee/`), the enforcement response and what is deliberately not in scope. The PRD's section 6 table now marks which rows are RULED and which stay proposed, and its outage sentence - "counter unavailability fails open on limits" - is superseded by the ruled posture, with the shipped counting semantics stated exactly: distinct principals ever admitted, not a trailing 30-day window, because that window and its alias-churn resistance are still design work and an append-only table cannot prove them.


---
- **Typed authoring documents, their audit rows and the signing chain are persisted, and the legacy policy substrate has an operator import** (#3776, #3786 item 1, epic #3549). `migrations/enterprise/155` adds three org-scoped, FORCE-RLS, append-only tables - artifacts, activations and signing keys - so a published policy version, its activation record and the key that verifies it all outlive the process that produced them, and `GET /api/v1/typed-policies/settings` reports `persistence: "database"` once 155 is applied. It still reports `"process"` where it is not - the flag and the migration are turned on by different people, so one build serves both postures and the field is a READ of the deployment rather than a property of the release. Append-only is enforced three ways in migration 171's pattern: a row-level trigger (which binds the table OWNER, whom a privilege revoke does not), a statement-level TRUNCATE trigger, and a revoke of UPDATE/DELETE/TRUNCATE from both application roles - TRUNCATE separately, because it is a privilege distinct from DELETE and a FOR EACH ROW trigger does not fire on it at all. **The private signing key is deliberately NOT persisted**: a durable signing identity is #3605's KMS custody chain, so each process still mints its own key and records only the public half, which makes every artifact verifiable by every process without a second key-custody surface; `signing_key_custody` is reported separately from `persistence` so a reader cannot conclude that a key survives a restart because a policy does. A key can be withdrawn - the one permitted mutation is a revocation, column-scoped by grant and re-asserted by a trigger that also refuses un-revoking - and revocation takes effect on the read path, because the trust store is loaded only from unrevoked rows. **`axonflow-policy-import`** brings both legacy families into the model: a DRY RUN by default (the confirmation is a field on the write options, not a command-line convention, so a second caller cannot write by forgetting), idempotent on the document's SOURCE digest rather than the artifact digest, with one reported result per captured row including the disabled ones, which import as disabled rather than vanishing. **A superseded row can be STRONGER than the row that superseded it** - all five live pairs are, because migration 067 relaxed the system defaults to `warn` by category and by an explicit `sys_pii_*` id list and the pre-canonical spellings escaped both - so the import presents BOTH generations of every pair with both actions and the reason, imports both by default, and resolves a collapse by the STRONGER action rather than the newer row. Its ranking is separate from `agent.ActionRestrictiveness`, which ranks `deny` BELOW `log` at its default case; that function is the engine's behaviour and the ADR-065 shadow comparator reproduces it deliberately, so it is not changed here, and two guards with their own positive controls hold the two rankings together.
- **The portal dashboard's Total Policies tile is back, counting the policies in force** (#4152). The SaaS dashboard's tile reads only the portal's `GET /api/v1/typed-policies/active/summary`, the same count the orchestrator's route answers. It shows the total, how many policies are shipped and how many are the organization's own, how many policies of the shipped controls its document disabled, and that installed policy packs are not counted. Activating a document can lower the shipped count, as the summary route's entry explains. A count that cannot be read says why on the tile instead of showing zero. The portal refuses the count with `503 storage_unavailable` when a database is configured and its typed-authoring workspace fell back to the in-process store (#4271): that count would be the implicit baseline's while the organization's document is in force.
- **The MCP `list_policies` tool answers a count on Enterprise, where it answered `401`** (#4265). Its two reads carried no credential the routes admit: the loopback read of the agent's own static list, and the read of the dynamic list through the agent's orchestrator proxy. The static read now carries the internal-service credential `internalServiceHints` accepts, signed as the sibling forwarders sign theirs and scoped to the session's tenant and organization; the dynamic read goes through the existing orchestrator forwarder. On a deployment with no `AXONFLOW_INTERNAL_SERVICE_SECRET` the static read still answers on Community (the platform admits the public fallback token there), while the orchestrator refuses every caller by its own configuration; on Enterprise an unsigned read is refused by name rather than sent.
- **The same service-identity wording** in the Enterprise HITL module (`ee/platform/agent/hitl`), whose approval-grant code is deleted with the Community copy's. No other Enterprise-only change.
- **A response the governance plane withholds is not counted against the client's circuit breaker**: the caller did not cause it, and the same request from a client whose organization records no such constraint is still served. Every other orchestrator failure still counts.
- **A withdrawal of an organization's typed policy document now answers to rollback's authority** (#4299). Withdrawing returns the organization to the shipped set, and it was admitted for any holder of `policy:write` - including the author of the active document, who could not roll back to it. A withdrawal is now refused for the active document's author, as a rollback is, and an organization that enabled self-approval can still withdraw its own self-approved document while that grant holds. PRD v11 item 15 states the rule. A document whose signing key has since been revoked can still be withdrawn: the author is read from the version's admission record, not by loading the document. **Behaviour change:** an author who withdrew their own document alone must now have another eligible principal withdraw it.
- **The typed-policies responses now declare every member they send** (#4262). `GET /api/v1/typed-policies/edition` declares the vocabulary's identity (`catalog_digest`, `registry_version`, `catalog_fixture`); publish and activation declare `template_omissions` and `template_omissions_unavailable`; the activation record declares its nine members; the shipped-corpus view declares each control's `control`, `dynamic` and `name` and each obligation's six members; and the tier-limit refusal declares the `policy` that crossed the ceiling. A client generated from the specification can now read what the platform sends, which is what five SDKs had to read out of the platform's source instead.
- On a verifying (Enterprise) deployment, a user token stamped with the per-user issuer `axonflow-user-token-mint` must carry an `exp` at least one second after the epoch, `email`, `jti` and an `org_id` equal to the authenticating credential's organization, or it is refused before any policy: with HTTP 401 and `Invalid user token: per-user token invalid: <claim>` on `/api/request`, `/api/v1/decide`, the gateway pre-check and the MCP query, execute and check routes, which admitted it before (the MCP-server and proxied-REST planes already refused it); tenant-kind tokens (no issuer) are unchanged. (#4311)
- On the workflow step gate a held step is queued with the engine's typed approval requirement in the queue row's `request_context`: plane, decision_id, `approval_clauses` (one element per clause, each with its own quorum and eligible groups), `separation_of_duties`, and `expires_at` when the requirement declares an expiry. The row expires when the approval does; with no declared expiry it keeps the queue's default. First-class queue fields for the quorum and the eligible set are a v11.1.0 row.
- Every held step on the workflow step gate is queued with severity low in v11.0.0: severity derives from the risk score, which is computed from the request's content, and the gate presents none. A policy can no longer set it. The gate carries the risk score onto the approval it creates, so held-step severity will follow the risk score once the gate presents content (a v11.1.0 row).
- A step whose approval expired before it could be queued is withheld with reason `approval_expired`, naming the decision and the expiry; no approval is queued.
- Approving a workflow step (`POST /api/v1/workflows/{id}/steps/{step_id}/approve`) after its approval expired is refused with 409, error `approval_expired`, code `APPROVAL_EXPIRED`. When the expiry cannot be read, the approval is refused with 503, error `approval_state_unreadable`, code `APPROVAL_STATE_UNREADABLE` (fail closed). The plan-step approve (`POST /api/v1/plans/{id}/steps/{step_id}/approve`) answers both refusals 409, with an error text beginning `approval_expired:` or `approval_state_unreadable:`. A step with no queue row declares no expiry and is approved as before.
- v11.0.0 records who approved, releases the hold, and refuses an approval after its expiry on every approve path (409 approval_expired, with code APPROVAL_EXPIRED on the workflow step approve; that approve also fails closed with 503 approval_state_unreadable, code APPROVAL_STATE_UNREADABLE, when the expiry cannot be read, which the plan-step approve answers with 409; decide's approve answers 409 "request has expired"; plan resume answers both as 500 (a named refusal with the wrong status, #4249 row https://github.com/getaxonflow/axonflow-enterprise/issues/4249#issuecomment-5674231306)); the typed approval's eligible pool, quorum and separation of duties are recorded on the queue row (request_context) for the reviewer but enforced by no approve path (pre-existing on decide; v10's dynamic hold enforced no eligibility either, so no regression in strength).
- The multi-agent plane's per-step policy check is decided by the anchored engine, with no content presented. A policy that requires approval pauses the step with the typed approval requirement (plane `map`, decision_id, `approval_clauses`, `separation_of_duties`, and `expires_at` when declared). Approving a multi-agent step paused in memory after its approval timed out is refused with 409, with an error text beginning `approval_expired:`, and the execution stays paused. An approval that had already timed out when the step was checked withholds the step as `approval_expired`.
- The multi-agent plane now fails closed: with no enforcer, an unavailable decision, a refused subject or a step type the plane does not map, the step is withheld and the cause named. It proceeded before.
- A conditional step that carries no branch steps is not presented to the engine on any execution mode, and is skipped. A multi-agent workflow definition containing a conditional step with branch steps is refused before any step runs, on plan execute, plan resume and workflow execute: plan resume refuses it before any approval, aborts the workflow, and writes a blocked audit row with plane `map`. Branch steps will be presented to the engine by their own type in v11.1.0.
- In step mode, a plan whose first step's type the multi-agent map does not name is refused before its workflow is created, as confirm mode refuses it.
- The orchestrator's "WCP HITL ... disabled by licence tier" boot line now says a require_approval step is withheld (capability_requires_upgrade) before any enqueue, creating no reviewer entry. It says that during a declared licence transition the step is held and reports approval_enqueue=tier_disabled. Operators who grep for the old wording should grep for "disabled by licence tier" (case-insensitive), which both versions carry.

### CI / Testing (this repository only)
- **The CI fleet's Go build caches have a size cap, and the fleet probe reports the host's disk, its caches and every slot's checkout** *(CI / Testing)* (#4182). Each of the fleet host's eight runners kept a private Go build cache that only an age trim bounded, and under continuous load nothing got old enough to go: each reached 46-57 G and the root volume 97%. `infrastructure/ci-runners/runner-cache-cap.py` runs hourly and after the daily reaper's age tiers, and evicts each slot's least recently used cache entries from 20 G down to 15 G, never touching anything used in the last hour. It writes a status file that `runner-fleet-health.yml`'s probe job now reads: the job fails, and so opens a main-red issue, when the cap has stopped running, the disk is under 15% free, a slot is still over its cap, or any slot's checkout is sparse (the partial-tree class #4195 fixed at its source). The module caches are still bounded by nothing; their directory-level trim is #3922. The ledger lint's temp-file template no longer ends in `.py`, which BSD `mktemp` took literally, so one leftover file failed every later local run.
- **`3636_forcerls_grants` allows an owner-written FORCE-RLS table from a ledger checked both ways, instead of demanding INSERT on every one** *(CI / Testing)* (#4229). Main had been red on the production-posture registry's 3636 check [2] since #4221 (`8c4d01c4b`): `migrations/core/183` creates `typed_policy_import_drafts` with FORCE row level security and gives the application role SELECT and a column UPDATE but no INSERT, by design, because its only writer is the agent's boot step on the owner connection (`importPolicyOverrideDrafts(migrationDB)`). The suite's rule, SELECT and INSERT for every forced table, predated the first such table. Granting INSERT would widen the role for no caller, so the rule takes a closed exception instead: `runtime-e2e/3636_forcerls_grants/owner_written_tables.tsv`, with the readiness ledger's conventions, names the table, its migration and its sole writer, and `render_privileges.py` requires SELECT alone of a listed table. It still fails an unlisted table without INSERT and a listed table without SELECT, and it fails a stale row: a table not forced on the deployment, a table the role can INSERT into by a table or a column grant, a migration that does not create the table, a writer file that does not define the function, or any other non-test Go file whose source INSERTs, MERGEs or COPYs into the table (a lexical census; the writer's owner connection is pinned by `TestTheBootPathRunsTheOverrideImportAfterTheEnforcer`). So `definition-of-done.yml` (subscribed to `edited` for its body-reading gate) re-ran its three runtime-e2e/ lints on every body edit (746 runs against 544 pushes over 2026-09-08..11); `regression-test-required.yml` (subscribed to `edited`/`labeled`/`unlabeled` for its label-reading presence gate) re-ran the whole regression suite on every label click (884 runs); and `test.yml` subscribed to `labeled` with no job reading a label, re-running the whole Test Suite on an unchanged head (655 runs). The three lints move, job names byte-identical, to `runtime-e2e-lints.yml`, which never hears `edited`; the suite moves to `repository-gates.yml`; `test.yml` drops `labeled`. A job-level `if: github.event.action != 'edited'` was the rejected shape: a skipped job still creates a check run on the same head sha, the latest run per name is the one the ruleset reads, and a skipped required context is satisfied - so a body edit would have turned a red required lint green. `technical-docs/ADR-065-GATE-19-THREAT-MODEL.md` claimed ~30 rows were covered on any pull request carrying the `ci:full` label; the Enterprise-Tagged lane has refused `pull_request` since 2026-09-04, so those rows are now marked covered (post-merge), and the same claim is corrected in `enforcedRealPGLane` and the gate-17 budgets page it renders into, which `TestGate17GraphBudgetTableMatchesThePublishedDocument` keeps in agreement.

- **The pull-request board stops paying a hosted minute per trivial job: one-minute gates folded into one job, bookkeeping moved or scoped, and a guard on the per-push cost** *(CI / Testing)*. Measured over 2026-09-08..11 the PR tier billed 30,064 hosted minutes (~$1,353 per 30 days at the billed $0.006/min), and most of it was not work: GitHub rounds every hosted JOB up to a whole minute, so one-minute gates, change detectors and summaries billed more than many of the lanes around them. Forbidden files, telemetry markers, the expression-length guard, version alignment, tests hygiene, stale model ids and gitleaks' PR leg are now steps of ONE job, `repository-gates.yml`, on the self-hosted fleet, each step named for its old check and run `if: !cancelled()` so one red cannot hide another; `gitleaks.yml` keeps its push-to-main leg and both call `.github/scripts/gitleaks-delta-scan.sh`. `commit-lint`, `check-regression-test`, the partner-name denylist, `check-protected-changes` and both Contract Guards jobs moved to the fleet (none is required and nothing on the required path waits for them; Contract Guards installs into a per-job venv). `lint.yml`'s five repository guards became one hosted job still feeding `Lint Summary`, replayed on the staged mirror with `REPLAY_EVIDENCE_MIN=4`, a new replay knob so one guard's verdict line cannot stand in for the others. Java Examples Compile gained a workflow-level `paths:` equal to its detector (it gates no required context); Dependency Review runs only when a dependency manifest changed; `build.yml`'s detector is merge-queue-only (the pull_request trigger stays, because it is the only producer of the required `Build Summary`); Suite Gate's PR leg is a job-level skip. Serial and required-path jobs stay hosted, because the fleet's cost is queue time (p90 6.2 minutes on 2026-09-10) and only a serial job puts it on the critical path. `pr_board_hosted_cost_test.sh` prints the per-push board (at most 25 hosted jobs across 14 unfiltered workflows), caps an unfiltered workflow at 3 hosted jobs unless its count is pinned with a reason, refuses a pull_request trigger on any measured-heavy suite (closing the gap `no_pr_trigger_for_stack_booting_suites_test.sh` leaves for `sdk-smoke-tests.yml`), and pins the Java filter to its detector.

FROM` and `TRUNCATE`), and requires each handler it reaches to call `legacyfreeze.Answer`. Real-Postgres tests drive both surfaces as `axonflow_app_role` and as the owner, and `3039_rls_blind_reads` section 12 and `3059_dynamic_policy_list_tenant_scope` drive them on the production-posture stack.

- **The organization-root ceiling is now driven across the agent seam, because the proof that already existed runs where no reviewer looks** (#3973 / #4009; `runtime-e2e/3593_tier_scale_limits` arm C). `platform/orchestrator/typed_authoring_limit_realpg_test.go` drives N-1/N/N+1 against a real Postgres and is the better test of the arithmetic — and its lane, `unit-tests-enterprise-realpg`, carries `github.event_name != 'pull_request'` (`test.yml:1322`; the policy is stated in that file's header at line 11). On a merged PR it concludes **`skipped`** while the required `Test Summary` goes green, so a regression in the ceiling would not red any board a reviewer consults.

  **And an in-process test cannot see the seam.** `/api/v1/typed-policies` is served by the orchestrator and reached by customers through the agent, which stamps `X-Org-ID` from the cryptographically validated licence. A refusal whose status, reason or code does not survive that hop is a defect no in-process coverage can observe. `1431_policy_path_alias` publishes across this seam but asserts only the *reported* ceiling (`max_documents`); it never drives a refusal.

  **What the leg asserts, and why each part is there.** A document of exactly 50 policies publishes successfully FIRST — a refusal test that never observes a success is satisfied by a route that refuses everything, including a 503 for a vocabulary the stack forgot to configure. One policy over the ceiling is then refused **by reason** (`reason:"tier_limit"` plus `ERR_TIER_LIMIT_ORG_ROOT_POLICY`), not by status: the same code covers a ceiling and an unreachable ledger, so a 402 alone is equally consistent with a database blip — `Retry-After` is what separates them, and its absence is asserted. Finally the ledger count is **unchanged** by the refused publication, which is #3973's headline: before the fix a 21-policy document refused at a ceiling of 20 left 19 rows behind, so the organization sat at its ceiling with nothing in force.

  **Two changes the leg needed that are not assertions.** The suite now boots with `AXONFLOW_TYPED_AUTHORING_CATALOG=deployment` — a **stack change**, not a test change: without it the route answers 503 `catalog_not_configured` and the legs would assert that 503. And arm C's existing `principal_admissions` count, which compared every dimension against a humans+services constant, is now scoped to the two dimensions it means; it passed only because the new legs run after it, and an assertion whose correctness depends on statement order is one edit from being wrong.

  The base document is pinned by `platform/shared/authoringvocabulary/e2e_fixture_test.go` like 1431's and 3564's, so a change to the wire format breaks that test rather than this suite at 2am; the N-rule bodies are derived from it mechanically, with the gauntlet expectation built from the generated ids rather than written beside them.

Phase V sends admin create and delete, forgot, reset and change-password to `http://[::1]` with no forwarded header, a login and an admin read with `X-Forwarded-For: not-an-ip`, and one `AUTH_FAILURE` row PostgreSQL is made to refuse with a `NOT VALID` check. It asserts `::1` on every row, NULL for the malformed header with the login answering 200, and exactly one `event=audit_row_lost ... sqlstate=23514` line for the refusal, with no other lost row in the run. It names `[::1]` because `localhost` resolves to `::1` on macOS and to `127.0.0.1` on the Linux runners, so the defect showed on a laptop and never in CI. With this change the suite passes 35 of 35; with main's portal binary [A], [B], [E] and 9 of Phase V's 10 assertions fail. The floor rises from 25 to 35, and `audit/**` joins the suite's declared inputs.

- **The posture registry and the suite ledger now describe the legs #4036 added, so a reader of the row learns what the suite asserts** (#4036 follow-up; `scripts/e2e/production_posture_registry.txt`, `scripts/e2e/runtime_e2e_suites.tsv`). #4036 gave `3039_rls_blind_reads` a section asserting that the deprecated `/api/v1/dynamic-policies` family and its `/api/v1/tenant-policies` successor both answer 409 `LEGACY_POLICY_WRITE_FROZEN` with reads still 200, and changed `3059_dynamic_policy_list_tenant_scope` to seed its two tenant fixtures as the database OWNER because the portal create it used to perform is now refused. Neither row said so. A registry row is the only description most readers see, and a row describing a suite that no longer works that way sends someone to the wrong file when it reds.

- **The over-threshold gate poll re-requested an idempotent key thirty times, so it could never observe the policy it was waiting for** (#4048 follow-up; `runtime-e2e/3039_rls_blind_reads`). `Service.StepGate` defaults to `RetryPolicyIdempotent`, whose contract is stated in its own source: *"Same (workflow_id, step_id) returns the same decision unless the caller explicitly requests a fresh evaluation via retry_policy=reevaluate."* On a hit it returns `buildCachedResponse` - the persisted `workflow_steps` verdict, stamped `cached=true` / `decision_source="cached"` - after bumping `gate_count`. When #4048 moved this suite's seed from the portal API (which triggers a synchronous `PolicyService.RefreshPolicies()`) to a direct `psql` insert (which does not), the first gate call could land ahead of the engine's 30s ticker, persist `allow`/`No matching policies`, and freeze that answer. Posture run 34593191501 shows the result exactly: `decision_source=cached`, `gate_count=30`, after 90s of polling that could not have recovered at any duration. The poll now sends `retry_policy=reevaluate`, which is what `runtime-e2e/3281_wcp_stepgate_segment` already does for the same reason - its comment says the loop "relies on reevaluate to see the dynamic-policy cache's next refresh rather than replaying a cached decision".

  **The failure message was the more expensive half.** It appended *"the gate cache is empty under RLS (#3039 bug C, the production policy-bypass)"* to every failure of this assertion, regardless of cause - so an idempotent replay was reported as a production policy-bypass, and two people spent hours chasing one. The boot log had ruled it out all along: the gate-cache refresh pool connects as `axonflow_platform_admin` (BYPASSRLS), which makes `refreshPoolIsRLSScoped` false and the #3039 mechanism inapplicable. The message now states what was observed - decision, reason, `decision_source`, `gate_count` - and lists candidate causes cheapest-first, with the RLS one qualified by the boot-log line that would have to be true for it to apply. A diagnostic that names a subsystem it never verified is the same defect class as a capture that welds `INSERT 0 1` onto an id.

  Both are pinned by `tests/regression-test-required/posture_seed_capture_validates_its_value_test.sh`, which fails against the pre-fix suites (6 checks red) and passes against the fixed ones (15 green).

- **A posture-suite seed welded psql's command tag onto the policy id it captured, so two suites reported a correct subsystem broken** (#4048 follow-up; runtime-e2e/3039_rls_blind_reads, runtime-e2e/3059_dynamic_policy_list_tenant_scope). `psql -tAc` with `RETURNING policy_id` writes the row AND the `INSERT 0 1` command tag, and the capture piped both through `tr -d ' \n'`. Posture run 34573411294 seeded a policy and captured `e2e-3059-tenant-a-...-6972INSERT01`; 3039 then failed with "policy list does not contain the policy seeded moments ago" while the response body in the very same log line plainly contained the policy, and 3059's poll spent its full 90s failing to match a list that was serving the row. Two of the suite's fifteen legs were red for this and nothing else.

  **The guard is the fix, not the flag.** Both captures tested only `[ -n "$id" ]`, and `e2e-...INSERT01` is non-empty, so the corrupted value passed at the seed and surfaced as an unrelated assertion failure ninety seconds downstream — a true-looking failure naming the wrong subsystem, which is the most expensive shape of wrong. The capture is now asserted EQUAL to the `policy_id` it seeded, which fails at the seed and names the cause. Planted positives: a tag on the first line, a leading `NOTICE:`, and a wrong id are each killed by the equality assertion and were each accepted by the old `-n` guard.

  **`sed -n '1p'` rather than `head -1`, and the precedent does not transfer.** `head` closes the pipe after one line, so psql can take SIGPIPE writing the tag; under these two files' `set -euo pipefail` that aborts the suite ON the seed line with status 141. Measured: `head -1` returns 141 where `sed -n '1p'` returns 0, because sed reads to EOF and has no race. psql's two lines normally fit the pipe buffer so head usually wins — "usually" is the flake. `3509_policy_authored_hitl`'s `psql_q` does use `head -1` and is correct there only because that suite runs `set -uo pipefail`, without `-e`.

- **Runtime legs for the per-scope corpus: `3564_per_plane_decision_shadow` Phases E and E2 and the incident lever** *(CI / Testing)* (#4046). Phase E asserts `decide` allows a query carrying an SSN with no `redact_pii` obligation under `enforce`, and the incident lever asserts the legacy engine gives the same verdict. Phase E2's prompt-injection row is now released with the marker stripped, byte-identical to the off leg, and nothing is counted as withheld `explicit_constraint`. Floor 89 -> 91. Its row in `scripts/e2e/runtime_e2e_suites.tsv` describes the legs.

- **Two production-posture suites stopped failing on a refusal that is now the contract** (#4036). `3039_rls_blind_reads` and `3059_dynamic_policy_list_tenant_scope` each created a dynamic policy through the portal's now-frozen route, so both failed deterministically on main on every posture run. They seed the fixture as the database owner instead and assert the 409 **in addition** - not by inversion. Expecting the refusal in place of the create would have deleted what those suites exist to prove: 3039's read-back and over-threshold gate is the production policy-bypass test, and 3059's two separately-owned rows are the cross-tenant invisibility test. A suite that stops creating them stops testing isolation. (The issue text asked for the inversion; this is a correction to it.)

- **The seven real-Postgres migration proofs that took a DSN from the environment now provision their own database, and the wiring census's exemption list is empty** *(CI / Testing)* (#4034, follow-up to #4021). They read `TEST_DATABASE_URL` (four) or `DATABASE_URL` (three) and `t.Skip`ped without one, so they could not be named in `migrations-gate.yml` — the gate sets no DSN, and seven names that SKIP every run would red the paired `^--- PASS:` assertion for a reason unrelated to any change. They were exempted in the census with exactly that reason, which is a decision rather than an omission — and they ran **nowhere on the `pull_request` tier**, because the only lane that executed them (`Unit Tests: Enterprise-Tagged + Real-PG`) is post-merge.

  `platform/agent/migration_realpg_harness_test.go` is what closed it, and it is **two** harnesses because the seven are two classes. `migrationTestDB` serves the four that reset the schema and apply their own range (104, 105/106, 107, 117): they were already hermetic *given* a superuser database of their own, and the database was the only thing missing. **Neither harness reads a DSN from the environment**, which is not a preference — a helper that runs `DROP SCHEMA public CASCADE` must own the database, and the first version of this file reused a helper that falls back to `DATABASE_URL`. It also carries `SetMaxOpenConns(1)`, which all four set one line apart and which is load-bearing rather than tuning — these tests set session GUCs and then apply migrations that read them, and with a pool the apply can land on a different connection than the `set_config` did.

  `migrationSchemaDB` serves the three schema-sanity proofs (076 ×2, 082), which had a **second, independent** reason to be unwireable: each additionally `t.Skipf`'d on an absent table. That is the right answer against an arbitrary environment database and the wrong one against a database the harness itself migrated, where "the table is not there" is the finding. The skip is now a failure — a skip reads as a pass to `go test`'s exit code, to the gate, and to every counter except the by-name `--- PASS` assertion.

  **`gateWiringExemptions` is now empty**, so the census's claim is unqualified: all **77** migration-subject real-Postgres tests in `platform/agent` and `platform/orchestrator` are named in the gate's `-run` filters and its PASS-assertion lists. The comment left in its place states the bar for adding an entry back — a reason must name an observable that would make the entry go away, not a difficulty.

- **Three compat mutants stopped testing anything when `prepareCredential` was extracted, and a fourth guard test shipped with no mutant at all** *(CI / Testing)* (#4035). `platform/shared/identity/compatmutation` was red on `main` under `-tags enterprise` from `1db5be6dd` (#4025): the anchors for *"an adapter-side defect enforces"*, *"a realm-source outage is reported as UNKNOWN_REALM"* and *"an outage is run through realm verification and reported as an unverified signature"* each matched zero times in `compat.go` after the preparation steps moved out of `Resolve`. The gate's own message is the rule followed here - **re-anchor, never delete**: a mutant deleted because its anchor moved removes the only evidence that the guard it names can fail.

  **Two of the three anchors follow the words; one follows the BEHAVIOUR, and the difference is the point.** The realm-outage branch and the unverifiable short-circuit moved bodily into `prepareCredential`, so their anchors moved with them. The adapter-defect mutant did not: what it asserts is what `Resolve` does with a defect *once preparation reports one* - record it, and never attach a refusal - which still lives in `Resolve`'s `if prep.defect` branch. Anchoring it in `prepareCredential` would have left a mutant that compiles, kills its test, and tests a different property.

  Both re-anchors needed a longer anchor than the moved line, and the uniqueness assertion is why that is known rather than guessed: `if in.UnverifiableReason != "" {` now appears **twice** in `compat.go` (the short-circuit and `validateLegacyAuth`'s reason check), and the defect branch's two-line sequence is unique only at its own indentation, because the sibling refusal branch writes the same `Subject` line with `classifyDivergence` and `refusalFor` between it and the record.

  **The coverage arm was red too, and the issue did not name it.** `TestAdmitDecisionSubjectRunsResolvesPipelineWithoutTheModeOrTheRecord` arrived with #4025 carrying no mutant and no exemption. It is mutated rather than exempted, because the property it asserts is exactly the kind a mutant can remove: the new mutant reinstates the identity axis's mode gate inside `AdmitDecisionSubject`, which refuses at `CompatModeOff` - half of the test's own loop, and the observable that separates *"reuses the pipeline"* from *"reuses `Resolve`"*.

  Verified locally by exact name under `-tags enterprise`, since the compatmutation shards report `skipped` on the `pull_request` tier and nothing runs them on `main`'s push event: `TestEveryCompatMutantEditIsUniqueAndPresent` green, and `TestEveryCompatGuardCanFail` green at **164/164 invocations run, 0 abandoned on budget, 6m10s** - with all four mutants above shown to KILL their guards. A mutant that fails to compile is classified separately by the harness (`mutantDidNotBuild`) and cannot be counted as a kill, which is what makes those four passes mean what they say.

- **Runtime legs for the MCP response pass's enforcing seam: `3564_per_plane_decision_shadow` Phases D and E2, and `1431_policy_path_alias`'s posture read** *(CI / Testing)* (#3564). 3564 Phase D asserts that check-output under `enforce` with no active document is byte-identical to the off leg, redacted content included, and labelled `engine=legacy`.
